docs.title: OpenInterceptor
docs.text:
OpenInterceptor is an open-source, moddable space-combat simulator engine, written in Rust, for macOS and Linux first (Windows kept buildable).

Its reference content is X-COM: Interceptor (MicroProse, 1998), the third game in the X-COM series after UFO Defense and Apocalypse. In the same way that OpenXcom and OpenApoc play their games, the engine reads the data from the player's own copy of the CD and plays it. No original content is in the repository, ever.

Goals, in priority order

  1. Modding first. The engine should make it easy to build a custom space simulator or campaign: new ships, weapons, stations, missions and a tech tree, written as data packs and scripts. The most likely use is a campaign that uses none of the original assets. Interceptor is the worked example that proves the engine is complete.
  2. Be an example of good Rust practice for a 3D application or game engine: clear layering, small dependencies, modules commented for a Rust beginner, and unit tests for all code. See Learn Rust with this codebase and Best practices.
  3. Play X-COM: Interceptor from the player's data on current systems.

The same order is in the repository's CLAUDE.md project rules.

Site version 0.11.0; Definition and Specification 1.0.0 (revision history).

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Stage 0 (foundation and format analysis) is complete. Stage 1 (the flight simulator testbed) is complete, signed off on 2026-11-10 — every original ship, station and cockpit flies or renders from the player's CD, an original-free pack plays without it, any original asset can be replaced by a mod file (with --extract producing editable copies), and cockpits can be HD repaints or 3D models. Stage 2 is in progress (build 0.2.2): one campaign at a time — the original interceptor or the original-free default campaign Perils of the Void — with ship systems, power, damage and repair, tractor, cloak, ECM, hyperspace, wingman orders and an in-game controls menu. See implementation status and the plan.

docs.title: How work flows: Rapid Prototyping
docs.text:
The project follows the Rapid Prototyping workflow (Workflows). Each user request becomes, in the same pass and before any code, a feature (F-…) on the Definition, then requirements (R-…) citing it on the Specification, then issues queued in sio citing those requirements. There are no approval gates; the definition and specification are a permanent record that moves ahead of the code. When the prototype is complete they seed the formal definition and specification of a production version, built through the SpecItOut fast track.

Definition and Specification 1.0.0 (2026-11-11): 79 features and 168 requirements, those for the code already built marked reverse-engineered. Until sio supports a prototype kind the project runs as kind: implementation with spec pointing at docs/specification (DEV-042).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The definition says what the player or modder gets from OpenInterceptor, and why. It is written in terms of features: a feature names an outcome ("a modder can replace any asset"), never the mechanism that delivers it. The specification turns each feature into testable requirements; the implementation builds them.

Definition version 1.0.0 (79 features). Changes are listed in the change history.

docs.title: Areas
docs.text: Area Code Features Covers Flight FLT 7 How a craft moves: the flight model, speed management, the arena, hyperspace and, later, flight in an atmosphere. Combat CMB 11 Weapons, damage, ship systems, special equipment, targeting, wingmen and the enemies' behaviour. Cockpit & HUD HUD 8 What the pilot sees: cockpits, views, instruments and the targeting display. Controls & control console CON 9 How the pilot commands the craft: keyboard, mouse and gamepad bindings, finding the controls, and the tablet control console. Missions MSN 7 Battles with a purpose: roles, waves, objectives, outcomes, the debrief, environments and balance. Strategy & logistics STR 9 The real-time strategy game around the battles, and the default campaign's supply-chain logistics. Campaigns CPN 7 The campaigns that ship with the engine, how one is chosen and played, and what turns battles into a story. Background on each campaign is in the pages beside this one. Modding toolkit MOD 8 What a modder gets: packs, readable rule files, asset replacement, translation, conditions and the tools that check and generate content. Compatibility (original data) CMP 4 Playing X-COM: Interceptor from the player's own CD, read as data, without the project ever holding original content. Platforms PLT 4 Where OpenInterceptor runs and how it is shipped. Testbed & tools TST 5 The testbed that every stage ends in, the viewers, headless runs and the asset generators.

docs.title: Reading a feature
docs.text:
Each feature is a heading F-<AREA>-NNN Title with:

  • What the player or modder gets, and Why;
  • Status: implemented, in-progress or planned;
  • Source: the user's request, quoted where known, or the plan item;
  • Specified by: the requirements that state it precisely.

Feature IDs are permanent: a feature that is dropped is marked so, never renumbered.

docs.title: Background
docs.text: The Campaigns pages describe the three campaigns that define "done" — the original Interceptor campaign, the original-free default campaign and Interceptor Remastered — and the game design that the mod formats implement.

docs.title: Cockpit & HUD
docs.text:
What the pilot sees: cockpits, views, instruments and the targeting display.

Requirements for these features: Cockpit & HUD requirements.

Feature Status F-HUD-001 Cockpits and views Implemented F-HUD-002 Mod cockpits: HD art and 3D models Implemented F-HUD-003 Flight instruments Implemented F-HUD-004 Targeting display Implemented F-HUD-005 Cockpit layout editor Implemented F-HUD-006 Drift display Planned F-HUD-007 Seeing other craft Planned F-HUD-008 Atmosphere instruments Planned

docs.title: F-HUD-001 Cockpits and views
docs.text:
What. Each hull has its cockpit; the pilot switches between cockpit, chase and external views, including a manually orbited chase camera.

Why. The original's views, on modern wide screens.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 1.9; DEV-006.
  • Specified by: R-HUD-001, R-HUD-002

docs.title: F-HUD-002 Mod cockpits: HD art and 3D models
docs.text:
What. A modder can replace a cockpit with high-resolution art in its own design space, or with a 3D model whose instruments sit on the dashboard.

Why. Modding first: HD and 3D cockpits in the manner of XWVM.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan items 1.17, 2.18 and 2.21; DEV-033.
  • Specified by: R-HUD-003, R-HUD-004

docs.title: F-HUD-003 Flight instruments
docs.text:
What. Radars with shield rings, speed, energy, shield and hull gauges, power and system readouts, multi-function display pages and a message line.

Why. The pilot must always know the craft's state.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan items 1.9, 2.17 and 2.20; DEV-037.
  • Specified by: R-HUD-005, R-HUD-006

docs.title: F-HUD-004 Targeting display
docs.text:
What. Brackets on the target, a lead marker, lock indication, an off-screen arrow and a nav-point marker.

Why. Gunnery and navigation in three dimensions.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 1.9.
  • Specified by: R-HUD-007

docs.title: F-HUD-005 Cockpit layout editor
docs.text:
What. In the cockpit view the pilot or modder can move and resize instruments, place them on a 3D cockpit, and save the result as an addon.

Why. Modding first: instruments placed by eye, saved as data.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 2.22 (user feedback).
  • Specified by: R-HUD-008

docs.title: F-HUD-006 Drift display
docs.text:
What. The speed indicator shows forward speed and the sideways and vertical drift, with a flight-path marker showing where the craft is actually going.

Why. User request: "Indicator displaying current speed should display both X and Y since the physics system allows sideways drift."

  • Status: planned
  • Source: User request (feedback); interlude item F.1.
  • Specified by: R-HUD-009

docs.title: F-HUD-007 Seeing other craft
docs.text:
What. Other fighters are easy to see at combat ranges, and the player can set the picture's brightness.

Why. User request: "it is difficult to see other fighters"; a brightness level.

  • Status: planned
  • Source: User request (feedback); interlude item F.3.
  • Specified by: R-HUD-010, R-HUD-011

docs.title: F-HUD-008 Atmosphere instruments
docs.text:
What. In an atmosphere the HUD shows altitude, vertical speed and a horizon.

Why. Needed to fly over terrain.

  • Status: planned
  • Source: Plan item 3.6.
  • Specified by: R-HUD-012

docs.title: Combat
docs.text:
Weapons, damage, ship systems, special equipment, targeting, wingmen and the enemies' behaviour.

Requirements for these features: Combat requirements.

Feature Status F-CMB-001 Beam weapons Implemented F-CMB-002 Missiles and mines Implemented F-CMB-003 Damage and ship systems Implemented F-CMB-004 Power management Implemented F-CMB-005 Special equipment Implemented F-CMB-006 Targeting Implemented F-CMB-007 Wingmen and orders Implemented F-CMB-008 Enemies driven by data, with difficulty levels Implemented F-CMB-009 Stations with modules Implemented F-CMB-010 Damage looks, debris and explosions In progress F-CMB-011 Shot physics Planned

docs.title: F-CMB-001 Beam weapons
docs.text:
What. Beam weapons draw energy, fire at their own rate and can be linked to fire singly, in pairs or all together.

Why. The original's gunnery model; energy makes power management matter.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 1.6.
  • Specified by: R-CMB-001, R-CMB-002

docs.title: F-CMB-002 Missiles and mines
docs.text:
What. Missiles need a lock and home in; special missiles sidestep, decoy, wait cloaked, split or copy a ship; mines blow up when an enemy comes near.

Why. Every weapon of both campaigns must fight as described.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan items 1.6 and 2.10.
  • Specified by: R-CMB-003, R-CMB-004, R-CMB-005

docs.title: F-CMB-003 Damage and ship systems
docs.text:
What. Hits strike the shield facing the attacker, then armour, then hull. Damage that gets through knocks out ship systems, which damage control repairs; a craft without engines and manoeuvring drifts disabled.

Why. The original's damage model; disabled ships can be captured.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 2.5.
  • Specified by: R-CMB-006, R-CMB-007

docs.title: F-CMB-004 Power management
docs.text:
What. The pilot shares a power budget between beams, shields and switched-on equipment, transfers energy and balances the shields fore and aft.

Why. A piloting function of the original game.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 2.6; DEV-024.
  • Specified by: R-CMB-008

docs.title: F-CMB-005 Special equipment
docs.text:
What. Tractor beam (tow and capture), cloak, ECM, point defence and sensor and jamming probes work in battle, for the player and for AI pilots.

Why. All are equipment of the original game; probes and point defence give both campaigns tactical depth.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan items 2.7 and 2.10.
  • Specified by: R-CMB-009, R-CMB-010, R-CMB-011, R-CMB-012, R-CMB-013

docs.title: F-CMB-006 Targeting
docs.text:
What. The pilot cycles targets, picks the nearest hostile or the one in the sights.

Why. A piloting function of the original game.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 1.7.
  • Specified by: R-CMB-014

docs.title: F-CMB-007 Wingmen and orders
docs.text:
What. Wingmen fly in formation and obey orders from a comms menu: attack my target, fire at will, evasive, retreat, status report.

Why. A piloting function of the original game.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan items 1.8 and 2.16; DEV-018 (resolved).
  • Specified by: R-CMB-015

docs.title: F-CMB-008 Enemies driven by data, with difficulty levels
docs.text:
What. Every enemy type flies a behaviour written as data, with skill, fire discipline and use of its systems, and is harder or easier by difficulty level.

Why. Modding first: a modder writes new enemies without code. The original's AI is code, so its behaviours are derived.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan items 2.8 and 2.9; DEV-031, DEV-032.
  • Specified by: R-CMB-016, R-CMB-017

docs.title: F-CMB-009 Stations with modules
docs.text:
What. Stations carry turrets, shield generators and other modules at attachment points; destroying the hub takes the modules with it.

Why. Base assaults and defences of both campaigns.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 2.11.
  • Specified by: R-CMB-018

docs.title: F-CMB-010 Damage looks, debris and explosions
docs.text:
What. A craft looks more damaged as it is hurt, breaks into debris and explodes; stations can be shown under construction.

Why. Feedback on what the guns are doing; construction stages serve logistics.

  • Status: in-progress
  • Source: Plan items 2.2–2.4 (XSPT sprite explosions and model-set extras deferred).
  • Specified by: R-CMB-019, R-CMB-020

docs.title: F-CMB-011 Shot physics
docs.text:
What. Shots leave the gun with the craft's own motion, so while the craft turns they still appear to fire forwards in a straight line relative to the pilot. Once fired, a shot is independent of where the craft points.

Why. User request: "Weapons, when fired, should start with the same angular momentum as the craft so that they appear to fire forwards in a straight line relative to the player." Decision D1 (2026-11-11): a rules option, physics by default.

  • Status: planned
  • Source: User request (feedback); decision D1; interlude item F.2.
  • Specified by: R-CMB-002, R-CMB-021

docs.text: Version Date Change 1.0.0 2026-11-11 Bootstrap: F-CMB-001 – F-CMB-011 (11 features)

docs.title: Compatibility (original data)
docs.text:
Playing X-COM: Interceptor from the player's own CD, read as data, without the project ever holding original content.

Requirements for these features: Compatibility (original data) requirements.

Feature Status F-CMP-001 Play from the player's own CD Implemented F-CMP-002 Original formats read faithfully In progress F-CMP-003 No original content in the project Implemented F-CMP-004 Deviations on the record Implemented

docs.title: F-CMP-001 Play from the player's own CD
docs.text:
What. The engine finds the player's copy of the CD data and plays X-COM: Interceptor from it.

Why. Compatibility objective; the project never holds original content.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan items 1.1, 1.13 and 1.14.
  • Specified by: R-CMP-001, R-CMP-002

docs.title: F-CMP-002 Original formats read faithfully
docs.text:
What. Original meshes, textures, images, sounds, rules and text are read as data and shown as the original intended; sprites and video follow.

Why. Compatibility objective.

  • Status: in-progress
  • Source: Plan item 1.1; Stage 0 analysis; XSPT and Smacker outstanding (2.4, 6.3).
  • Specified by: R-CPN-012, R-MOD-019, R-CMP-003, R-CMP-004, R-CMP-005, R-CMP-006, R-CMP-007, R-CMP-008, R-CMP-009, R-CMP-010, R-CMP-011

docs.title: F-CMP-003 No original content in the project
docs.text:
What. Nothing from the original game is committed or published in any form; original binaries are read as data, never executed.

Why. Legal and ethical: the player supplies the data.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Project rules.
  • Specified by: R-CMP-012, R-CON-021

docs.title: F-CMP-004 Deviations on the record
docs.text:
What. Where the engine differs from the original, or uses its own value where the original's is unknown, the difference is documented and facts are marked verified, derived or unknown.

Why. An undocumented deviation looks like a bug.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Project rules; Deviations page.
  • Specified by: R-CMP-013

docs.title: Controls & control console
docs.text:
How the pilot commands the craft: keyboard, mouse and gamepad bindings, finding the controls, and the tablet control console.

Requirements for these features: Controls & control console requirements.

Feature Status F-CON-001 Rebindable keyboard, mouse and gamepad Implemented F-CON-002 Every original piloting function Implemented F-CON-003 One action catalogue, with a controls overlay Planned F-CON-004 Tablet control console Planned F-CON-005 Console target viewport Planned F-CON-006 Console 3D map Planned F-CON-007 Physical control panel Planned F-CON-008 Console function-group tiles Planned F-CON-009 Console themed by the active campaign Planned

docs.title: F-CON-001 Rebindable keyboard, mouse and gamepad
docs.text:
What. Every action can be bound to two keys and two gamepad buttons or chords, with device settings, from a controls menu in the launcher and the pause menu.

Why. Players and their hardware differ; a gamepad has far fewer buttons than the keyboard.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan items 1.10 and 2.15; DEV-003, DEV-004, DEV-028.
  • Specified by: R-CON-001, R-CON-003, R-CON-004, R-CON-005, R-CON-006

docs.title: F-CON-002 Every original piloting function
docs.text:
What. All piloting functions of the original game have a default key: power, tractor, cloak, ECM, hyperspace, wingman comms, message repeat.

Why. Compatibility: the original's keyboard layout and functions.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 2.16; DEV-001, DEV-027.
  • Specified by: R-CON-002

docs.title: F-CON-003 One action catalogue, with a controls overlay
docs.text:
What. A single catalogue of actions drives the key bindings, an in-flight overlay listing them, and the control console.

Why. User request: "There are a large number of keyboard shortcuts to keep track of."

  • Status: planned
  • Source: User request (feedback); interlude item F.5.
  • Specified by: R-CON-001, R-CON-007, R-CON-008, R-CON-011

docs.title: F-CON-004 Tablet control console
docs.text:
What. A web page served by the game turns a tablet on the local network into a second control surface beside a joystick or gamepad: live craft state goes out, the pilot's actions come back, in real time. The top row shows the exterior-view HUD; the centre a widened display console like the cockpit's; shield rings and shield controls sit on the left, power sliders on the right, and other functions grouped below. Off by default, local network only, paired with a code.

Why. Immersion, always knowing the craft's condition, and reaching features that are otherwise forgotten. Primary use: an iPad alongside a joystick or gamepad.

  • Status: planned
  • Source: User request; decision D2 (off by default; local network only; pairing code; port 8765, changeable); interlude items C1 and C2.
  • Specified by: R-CON-007, R-CON-009, R-CON-010, R-CON-011, R-CON-012, R-CON-013, R-CON-014

docs.title: F-CON-005 Console target viewport
docs.text:
What. The console's centre display shows the current target's model, turned to its true angle relative to the player.

Why. Knowing at a glance which way the target is facing.

  • Status: planned
  • Source: User request; interlude item C3.
  • Specified by: R-CON-015

docs.title: F-CON-006 Console 3D map
docs.text:
What. The console's centre display toggles to a 3D map of the battle, modelled on TIE Fighter's map view.

Why. Situational awareness without leaving the cockpit view.

  • Status: planned
  • Source: User request; interlude item C4.
  • Specified by: R-CON-016

docs.title: F-CON-007 Physical control panel
docs.text:
What. Longer term, a physical panel with lights and buttons (an Arduino over USB) works as a control console.

Why. Immersion for players who build their own cockpit.

  • Status: planned
  • Source: User request (longer term); interlude item C5.
  • Specified by: R-CON-010, R-CON-017

docs.title: F-CON-008 Console function-group tiles
docs.text:
What. The console's functions are grouped by ship system. Each group is a tile showing that system's status; tapping a tile opens a full-width strip with that group's controls and collapses the other tiles to their headers; tapping the open group's title closes the strip so every status card shows again; tapping another group's title switches the strip to that group. Every function group is shown for every craft; individual controls the current craft lacks (for example cloak or ECM not fitted, or no missiles) appear disabled and labelled as not fitted, and the status card shows those features as not fitted.

Why. User request (iPad UI): "since multiple options exist per function group, we will add a feature to make them easy to manage. The tiles present in the mockup will be used and show the status per system in the card. Tapping the tile will collapse other tiles to just their header, and present a full width strip with controls for that function group. Tapping title of the current view again collapses it so that the status cards are all visible. Tapping title of another function group switches the control display to that function group." User request: "Function groups not available at all for the current craft are not displayed. Available function groups are grouped at the horizontal screen center, with empty non-selectable groups where the remaining function group cards would usually be presented in same framing format but with no content." Superseded by the user: "actually based on design all are common, just with individual features disabled, so hiding the whole content is not necessary".

  • Status: planned
  • Source: User request (iPad UI); interlude item C2.
  • Specified by: R-CON-018, R-CON-019

docs.title: F-CON-009 Console themed by the active campaign
docs.text:
What. The console's look comes from the active campaign or mod. For Interceptor the console uses new assets made for this project, kept in the interceptor pack, styled after the current craft's cockpit overlay, with every control clearly labelled. The default campaign uses its retro (art-deco) style. No original art is reproduced in the console.

Why. User request: "The visual style of the tablet interface is derived from the active campaign/mod. In the case of X-Com Interceptor, these are new assets in the default mod, and the visual styling is based on the current craft's cockpit overlay, but with everything clearly labelled. The default campaign, likewise, follows the retro aesthetic."

  • Status: planned
  • Source: User request (iPad UI); interlude item C2.
  • Specified by: R-CON-020, R-CON-021

docs.title: Flight
docs.text:
How a craft moves: the flight model, speed management, the arena, hyperspace and, later, flight in an atmosphere.

Requirements for these features: Flight requirements.

Feature Status F-FLT-001 Newtonian flight, with an assisted option Implemented F-FLT-002 Flight computer: match and hold speed Implemented F-FLT-003 Afterburner and sideways thrust Implemented F-FLT-004 Arena boundary Implemented F-FLT-005 Hyperspace departure Implemented F-FLT-006 Collisions Implemented F-FLT-007 Atmospheric flight over terrain Planned

docs.title: F-FLT-001 Newtonian flight, with an assisted option
docs.text:
What. Every craft flies by thrust and momentum: it coasts when the throttle is off, slides through hard turns, slows with reverse thrust or a brake and is capped at its top speed. A campaign or mod may choose an arcade-style assisted model instead.

Why. A space simulator should feel like space; the arcade model of the first build slowed ships without thrust. Mods aiming at a different feel keep the choice.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 1.5; the owner's playtest of build 0.2.0 ("the arcade flight model slowed ships without thrust", Stage 1 plan).
  • Specified by: R-FLT-001, R-FLT-002, R-FLT-003, R-FLT-010

docs.title: F-FLT-002 Flight computer: match and hold speed
docs.text:
What. The pilot can match a target's speed and have the craft hold a forward speed while cancelling sideways drift. AI pilots fly with the same computer and the same limits.

Why. Newtonian flight is hard to manage in a dogfight without help; AI pilots must obey the player's physics to be fair.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 1.5; DEV-020.
  • Specified by: R-FLT-004

docs.title: F-FLT-003 Afterburner and sideways thrust
docs.text:
What. An afterburner raises top speed at an energy cost; craft with vectored thrust (VCT) can slide sideways and vertically.

Why. Both are piloting functions of the original game.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 1.5; original controls.
  • Specified by: R-FLT-005, R-FLT-006

docs.title: F-FLT-004 Arena boundary
docs.text:
What. A battle has an edge; a craft that reaches it is stopped there and told so.

Why. Under newtonian flight a coasting ship would otherwise drift away for ever.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 1.5; DEV-021.
  • Specified by: R-FLT-007

docs.title: F-FLT-005 Hyperspace departure
docs.text:
What. The pilot can jump out of a battle after a countdown, abort it, and take a craft held by the tractor along as a prize. Jumping out ends the battle as a retreat.

Why. Retreat and capture are part of the original game's battles.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan items 2.7, 2.16 and 3.8.
  • Specified by: R-FLT-008

docs.title: F-FLT-006 Collisions
docs.text:
What. Craft bounce off each other and off station hulls; fast shots never pass through a target.

Why. Stations are large solid objects, and hits must count.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 1.7.
  • Specified by: R-FLT-009

docs.title: F-FLT-007 Atmospheric flight over terrain
docs.text:
What. On planet surfaces craft feel drag, gravity and lift, can hover and land, and fly over terrain with ground installations, a sky and fog.

Why. New to this engine: it lets campaigns fight on worlds, not only in space (the default campaign has surface missions).

  • Status: planned
  • Source: Plan items 3.3–3.5.
  • Specified by: R-FLT-011, R-FLT-012

docs.title: Missions

Battles with a purpose: roles, waves, objectives, outcomes, the debrief, environments and balance.

Requirements for these features: Missions requirements.

Feature Status F-MSN-001 Missions as data Implemented F-MSN-002 Debrief Implemented F-MSN-003 Radio chatter and voices In progress F-MSN-004 Environments and hazards Planned F-MSN-005 Simulator missions Planned F-MSN-006 Base defence the player can win Planned F-MSN-007 Logistics missions In progress

docs.title: F-MSN-001 Missions as data
docs.text:
What. A mission is a data file: the forces taking part, when and where they arrive, waves, objectives, a timer, outcomes and chatter.

Why. Modding first: new missions without code.

  • Status: implemented

docs.title: Game design and mod format
docs.text: Status: design, version 1 draft (2026-11-10). Nothing in this section is implemented yet unless a page says so; the implementation plan schedules it. Pages written here are the reference the stages implement against: a key named here is the key the engine will read.

docs.title: The goal
docs.text:
OpenInterceptor is a general engine for space-combat strategy games: a real-time strategy layer (a star map, bases, research, an economy, factions) wrapped around a first-person space combat simulator. Everything a game is made of is a mod: a folder of rules, campaign definitions, scripts and assets.

Three mods define what "done" means:

Mod Kind What it proves interceptor campaign, needs the player's CD The format can express every system of the original game: the full X-COM: Interceptor campaign is the primary test case. default campaign, original-free The engine stands alone: a complete, smaller campaign — two factions competing for the resources of a few star systems — built only from content made for this project. It ships with the engine and is what runs when no CD is present. interceptor-remastered campaign with parent = interceptor A mod can extend another campaign and override individual assets: sharper textures for modern screens and an upgraded fighter model with real raised and recessed geometry.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text: Page Contents The original game, system by system A functional analysis of X-COM: Interceptor: every system, its rules, and where its data lives. Mod structure Mod kinds, parent, folder layout, load order, ids, overrides, generated assets. Format: campaign and game flow The campaign ruleset: start state, calendar, phases, difficulty, victory and defeat. Format: strategy layer Star map, factions and relations, economy, research, bases and modules, ships, equipment, pilots. Logistics Planned for the default campaign: resources and deposits, mining facilities, research stations, manufacturing centers, supply convoys and ambushes, survey ships, construction stages; open questions. Format: space objects and models Object descriptors, model sets (intact, damage, debris, construction states), mounts. Format: missions and events Mission types and generation, objectives, outcomes; scripted campaign events. Format: behaviours and scripting AI and object behaviours with difficulty variants; the condition/action language; scripts. Format: interface, text and media Screen layouts and skins, cockpits, text and encyclopaedia, music, video. Coverage matrix Every original system → the format construct that expresses it → its simplified equivalent in the default campaign. The Interceptor campaign mod How the interceptor mod defines the full original campaign from the CD. The default campaign Design of the original-free campaign, its content and how its assets are generated. Interceptor Remastered Asset recipes: upscaled textures and mesh patches built locally from the player's CD.

docs.title: Design principles
docs.text:
1. Data first, scripts second. Everything the original game does must be expressible as rules and declarative definitions (with a small condition language). Scripts exist for mods that want behaviour the declarative layer cannot describe; the interceptor and default campaigns must not need them. This keeps campaigns checkable by --check, saves deterministic, and modding approachable.
  2. One format for both campaigns. Every construct the original needs has a simpler use in the default campaign, and vice versa (coverage). A feature only one of them would use is a sign the format is shaped around a game rather than a genre.
  3. Extend what exists. The established conventions stay: YAML rules files (mod format 2, checked against schemas) with inherit (including inherit: original:<file>/<section> to read the original INI data), layering by load order, original: references, per-asset overrides at fixed paths, OBJ/PNG/WAV for mod art. New content types are new top-level sections and folders, not a new syntax.
  4. No original content in the repository. The interceptor mod is rules and references; the remastered mod is recipes that the engine applies to the player's own files.
  5. Everything is validated. Every reference, condition and expression is checked at load (--check) with a message naming the file, line and key path.

docs.title: The default campaign
docs.text:
Status: design; built up stage by stage (plan). First playable content delivered in Stage 2 (packs/default, which replaced the Stage 1 sample pack). Mod id default, kind campaign, no original content. Working title: Perils of the Void.

It is what the engine runs when no CD is present, the reference implementation of a complete campaign, and the template a modder copies to make their own. It uses every format construct the interceptor campaign uses, in a simpler form (coverage).

docs.title: Aesthetic: a 1950s film serial
docs.text:
The look and the story come from the science-fiction cinema serials and pulp magazine covers of the late 1940s and 1950s — as a genre, not any particular serial or character:

  • Ships: stylised rocket ships (needle and cigar hulls, swept tail fins, nose cones, porthole rows, chrome trim, exhaust bells) against flying saucers (domed discs, rim lights, antenna spikes) and tin-can robots. Low-poly forms with smooth shading and saturated two-tone paint.
  • Palette: rocket-red, cream, chrome and teal for the player; violet, acid green and black for the villain; Technicolor nebulae and painted-backdrop planets with rings.
  • Interface: art-deco panels, Bakelite knobs, radar scopes with phosphor green sweeps, Nixie-tube counters, ticker-tape messages; screen titles in poster lettering.
  • Story: told in chapters. Each opens with a title card ("Chapter 4: Trapped in the Ion Storm!") and a narrator's recap. Each ends on a cliffhanger: a special mission that begins at the worst possible moment. The next chapter resolves it.
  • Planets: battles also happen on worlds — jungle planets under violet skies, airless cratered moons — where rockets fly like aircraft: drag slows them, gravity pulls them down, and fights are slower and closer to the ground (environments).
  • Sound: theremin and organ stings, ray-gun zaps, rocket roars, a brassy title fanfare, all synthesised.

docs.title: Premise
docs.text:
The inner worlds are powered by cosmium, a glowing crystal found only in the asteroid belts and moons of six frontier systems. The Interplanetary Guard (the player) protects the mining colonies. From a dark moon at the edge of the map, Regent Vexor of the Umbral Dominion has begun building the Eclipse Engine: a colossal lens that, fed with enough cosmium, will cast the inner worlds into permanent night unless they kneel.

Both sides race to mine the belts, research new technology, build stations and fight for every system. The Regent needs cosmium for his Engine; the Guard needs it to stop him.

docs.title: Factions
docs.text:
Faction Role Kind Notes Interplanetary Guard The player player Rocket ships; bases with modules Umbral Dominion The opponent; its diabolical plan drives the campaign rival Saucers and robots; own economy, research tree, bases, strategist Solar Senate Third party: the government patron Funds the Guard per protected colony; can cut funding, demand missions, or (if relations collapse) recognise the Regent and stop funding altogether Nebula Cartel Third party: smugglers and traders independent Sells rare parts to whoever pays; secretly supplies the Dominion while relations with the Guard are poor; can be turned into an ally or broken Belt Prospectors Third party: free miners independent Their mines yield cosmium to whoever protects them Black Comet raiders Third party: pirates hostile Raid everyone; may be hired by the Cartel or the Regent

Relations are dynamic (format). Defending a faction's bases, convoys and ships raises its standing with the Guard; attacking them lowers it; and each faction's enemies react the opposite way. Over the campaign the player can make the Cartel an ally (its convoys then supply the Guard and stop supplying the Regent), lose the Senate's backing by neglecting its colonies, or drive the Prospectors into the Regent's arms. Stances change who fights alongside or against the player in battle, who trades, and which story branches open.

docs.title: Structure: chapters driven by both sides' progress
docs.text:
The campaign is one arc of 12 chapters. A chapter's cliffhanger mission is triggered by conditions on the player's progress and the Regent's plan, not by the calendar alone, so a strong player meets the story faster and a struggling one sees the villain advance.

The Eclipse Engine is a plan with three stages (Lens, Coils, Heart). Each stage needs shipments of cosmium and parts carried by saucer convoys, which the player can intercept, and the plan's progress is visible to every chapter condition.

Ch. Title (working) Cliffhanger triggered when Special mission Outcome 1 The Shadow Falls Campaign start Tutorial defence: saucers strike a mining colony Unlocks the star map, first base 2 Raiders of the Belt First mine built, or day 15 Convoy escort through raider space Prospectors' relation; cosmium income 3 The Regent's Ultimatum Dominion builds its 2nd base, or Guard researches 4 topics Broadcast intercept: catch a saucer carrying the Regent's message Reveals the Eclipse Engine; plan stage 1 begins 4 Trapped in the Ion Storm! Plan ≥ 15% and a Guard squadron is in deep space Survive: an ion storm cripples sensors while saucers attack Storm map hazard learned; derelict found 5 The Secret of the Derelict Chapter 4 done Surface salvage: the derelict has crashed on a jungle planet; fly down through the atmosphere and tractor it out under fire from saucers and ground robots Research: saucer propulsion 6 Senate in Peril Senate relation < 20 or plan ≥ 33% Defend the Senate station from a robot boarding fleet Senate relation ±; funding changes 7 The Cartel's Price Cartel relation crosses friendly or wary Choice: escort a Cartel shipment (Cartel ally) or raid it (cut the Regent's supply) Branches: Cartel ally or Cartel hostile 8 Lens of Doom Plan stage 1 complete Strike the lens assembly yard Delays stage 2 (or loses a colony) 9 The Traitor in the Guard Guard researches saucer propulsion and Dominion research ≥ level 2 Pursuit: chase a defector's stolen rocket before it reaches the Regent One rival research topic stolen or kept 10 Into the Dark Moon's Shadow Plan ≥ 66% or Guard holds 4 systems Surface recon: fly low over the dark moon's airless craters, under the fortress guns, to photograph the Engine site Map of the Engine site 11 The Eclipse Begins! Plan stage 3 starts Desperate defence: the Engine fires a test beam at a colony; save its people Colony saved or lost; Senate reaction 12 Duel at the Eclipse Engine Map found + atomic torpedo researched + flagship built Final assault, two parts: break the fleet, then fly into the Engine's core Victory (total or partial)

Victory: destroy the Eclipse Engine (total victory if the flagship survives, partial if it is lost). Defeat: the Engine completes; the Guard's last base falls; or the Senate withdraws recognition (funding at 0 for 60 days).

docs.title: Logistics: mines, research stations and foundries (planned)
docs.text:
Features: Strategy & logistics (F-STR-005 – F-STR-009).

The user has asked for the default campaign's strategy layer to run on supply lines (design; decisions recorded 2026-11-11):

  • New base types: mining facility, research station, manufacturing center, built in star systems according to their resources; research stations only in systems meeting a research site's criteria (a nebula, a pulsar…).
  • Supply and demand: the main base orders components (for fighters and other technology) from manufacturing centers; manufacturing orders materials from mining facilities; nothing is produced until its materials have arrived. Resources and components are campaign data.
  • Supply convoys are automatic, provided by the government, and travel the fixed lanes as convoys of several large vessels (a core vessel with attached cargo containers), each carrying an even share of the cargo, so a partly destroyed convoy still delivers the surviving share. Where along its route a convoy will be attacked is chosen at random at launch; destroyed cargo is lost, captured cargo goes to the Dominion's supply depots (destroy a depot to seize it).
  • Research stations open tech branches that ordinary bases cannot research (for example theremin shielding at a nebula lab); materials are needed only to begin a project.
  • Survey ships — a different mission and craft from supply ships — are sent to systems within the base's radar range to find which station types they suit; when one launches, a 25 % roll decides whether it will be attacked.
  • Fighters are built at main bases and transferred to a facility's own pool, defending it and escorting its supply ships.
  • Construction takes time and passes through three construction stages, each with its own mesh and debris (implemented: build_25 from 0 %, build_60 from 60 %, build_90 from 90 %, thresholds confirmed); from 50 % the Dominion may attack a facility under construction, at most three times per location.
  • Third-party convoys: Prospectors fly expeditions (to a system, pause, home); the Cartel's destinations are random, even uncharted stars.

This fits the premise — both sides race to mine the belts — and gives the Escort and Convoy raid mission types a strategic cause. The Regent's Eclipse Engine shipments use the same convoys. Owners: Stage 4 (economy and logistics), Stage 3 (convoy-ambush and construction-defence missions), Stage 5 (the Dominion's depots and third-party convoys). Already built in Stage 2: the facility and supply-craft objects, their construction-stage models and debris, and the construction-defence and convoy-ambush testbed arenas. Still open: supply-vessel cargo capacity (TBD, set by tech-tree balance) (design page). The interceptor campaign stays without logistics.

docs.title: The Interceptor campaign mod
docs.text: Status: design; authored across Stages 2–6, playable start to finish at the end of Stage 5. The existing interceptor pack grows into a kind: campaign mod that plays the whole original campaign from the player's CD. It is the primary test case of the engine: if a system of the original cannot be expressed, the format is incomplete.

docs.title: What the mod contains — and what it does not
docs.text:
The mod contains only this project's own work: rules that inherit original sections, definitions authored from the analysis, and references to original files. It never contains original text, art, audio or extracted tables of the original's content beyond the names and numbers needed to reference them (mesh names, section names, values the rules restate).

packs/interceptor/
  pack.yaml                    kind: campaign, requires_original: true, format: 2   (exists)
  campaign/
    campaign.yaml              campaign: (difficulty levels exist), starts:, endings
    doomsday.yaml              arcs: doomsday, plans: doomsday, warnings
    score.yaml                 scores: interceptor (MissionScores by name), reports
  strategy/
    map.yaml                   maps: frontier (generated); star_classes ×9; bodies; travel
    factions.yaml              xcom, alien, corporate (funding), pirates, cult, arms dealer, gsc
    economy.yaml               resources, incomes, expenses, markets, factories, deliveries, storage
    research.yaml              71 topics: inherit original:GameSettings.ini/R_*, + unlocks, appears
    salvage.yaml               13 sets: inherit the *Goodies sections
    bases.yaml                 base_types: xcom, alien; templates
    modules.yaml               68 modules: inherit M_*, + effects, on_destroyed, model sets
    items.yaml                 beams, launchers, missiles, mines, equipment: inherit originals
    pilots.yaml                pilots: ranks inherit RankAdvancement*, formulas authored
    strategist.yaml            strategists: alien — Think.ini values by reference + rules
  rules/                       combat rules (ships, weapons, systems, flight, cockpits, sounds;
                               exist as YAML today)
  models/
    modelsets.yaml             21 class model sets, 11 station sets, module sets with textures
    debris.yaml                the 28 debris sets
    effects.yaml               explosions, shock waves, shield rings
  behaviours/                  per-class AI with Beginner…Superhuman variants
  missions/                    27 mission types, simulator types, the final mission
  events/                      side missions, messages, news triggers, reports
  interface/                   screens laid out with original wrapper art; cockpits A/B/C
  text/en/                     imports: original:LangFile1.txt, starcorp1, Names1, news1, short1
  scenarios/                   testbed arenas (exist as YAML today, kept)

docs.title: Import, reference, author
docs.text: Kind of content How the mod gets it Numbers in GameSettings.ini, Think.ini, soundfx.ini, MPSettings.INI inherit: original:<file>/<section> (implemented; original keys map to field names by spelling, HitPoints → hit_points) and per-key references (think:<section>/<key>); never copied Text text: original:LangFile1.txt and the other text files, imported at load under orig.* keys; the mod's own text files only map ids to those keys Models, textures, images, sounds, music, video original: references and override paths (Stage 1) Tables the executable holds (class → mesh, debris sets, module texture triples, star visuals) Written as rules naming the original meshes and textures — facts needed to reference the data, recorded once in the mod Rules the executable holds (mission compositions, AI, story, yields, formulas) Authored from the analysis; each definition's comment cites its source (guide chapter, CD string, play-test) and confidence

docs.title: Id mapping
docs.text:
Original section names become readable ids, with the original name kept as the inheritance source:

research:
  tri_titanium:
    inherit: original:GameSettings.ini/R_<topic>   # level, file_size, prereq* (section name illustrative)
    size: "file_size * 1000"                 # the original's unit is k TQ
    requires: "research(wraith_examination)" # numeric Prereq ids resolved to readable ids
    unlocks: [items.tri_titanium_armor, hulls.firestar]   # AUTH: guide ch. 3
    name: "@orig.R_<topic>.found"            # from short1.txt

Numeric tech ids in prerequisite keys (Prereq1=12 in the original file) are translated by a mapping table in the mod (tech_ids:), checked by --check against the original file so a mistake is reported, not silently wrong.

docs.title: Fidelity process
docs.text:
1. Stage 2 — combat behaviours: each alien class's behaviour tuned against recorded play of the original (where possible) and the guide's descriptions; difficulty variants from the guide's list of what each level changes.
  2. Stage 3 — mission types: each of the 27 types authored; compositions from the guide's legible tables, else estimates marked derived; checked by playing each in the testbed.
  3. Stages 4–5 — the strategy layer, then the arc and the strategist; a full campaign play-through at Veteran is Stage 5's exit test, with a log comparing milestone dates (first message, first Firestar, Doomsday progress) against the guide's expectations.
  4. The open items are closed or documented as derived estimates in the mod.

docs.title: Interceptor Remastered
docs.text: Status: design; scheduled in Stage 7. The example of a campaign that extends another: parent: interceptor, plus sharper textures for modern screens and an upgraded X-1A Lightning II whose panel lines, vents and intakes — today only painted on — are real geometry.

docs.title: The constraint: nothing derived from the CD may be shipped
docs.text:
An upscaled original texture is a conversion of MicroProse's art, and so is a model built by editing the original Lightning mesh. Project rule: no original content, conversions included, enters the repository or a published mod. So the remastered mod ships recipes, and the engine produces the remastered assets on the player's machine from the player's own CD (generated assets). What is published is the mod's own work only: recipe files, patch instructions, and any art made from scratch.

mods/interceptor-remastered/
  pack.yaml                    kind: campaign, parent: interceptor, requires_original: true
  recipes/textures.yaml        upscale every original texture x4
  recipes/images.yaml          upscale the HUD and menu images x2 (cockpits: see below)
  recipes/lightning.yaml       build the enhanced Lightning from the original mesh
  patches/lightning.meshpatch  the face edits (this project's own work: numbers, no geometry)
  rules/models.yaml            point the Lightning's model set at the generated model

docs.title: Textures: the upscale generator
docs.text:
recipes:
  textures-x4:
    kind: upscale
    inputs: original:*.xtxr            # all 799 textures
    scale: 4
    method: edge-directed
    sharpen: 0.3
    output: "textures/{name}.png"      # = the texture override path, so it replaces the original

Method. The originals are 8-bit palettised and mostly 64–256 px: blocky edges and dithering are the problem, not a lack of high-frequency detail. The built-in, deterministic pipeline (all in-crate, no ML model, no dependency):

  1. Decode at full colour (palette 0; Stage 1 reader).
  2. De-dither: a small edge-preserving smoothing pass (a bilateral filter in a 3×3 window) removes the palette's ordered-dither noise without blurring panel edges.
  3. Edge-directed upscale ×2 per step (two steps for ×4): each new pixel is interpolated along the local edge direction (estimated from gradients) rather than across it — the idea behind NEDI/xBR-family scalers — so diagonal panel lines stay sharp and stair-free.
  4. Sharpen lightly (unsharp mask) and re-apply the colour key / alpha mask at the new resolution, with a 1-pixel feathered edge.
  5. Wrap-aware borders: the textures tile (Stage 1 found UVs outside 0..1), so filtering wraps around the edges instead of clamping, avoiding seams.

Each step is a pure function on an image buffer with unit tests on synthetic images (a hard diagonal edge stays a single sharp edge at ×4; a checkerboard dither becomes flat colour; a tiling texture stays seamless). Output quality is judged by a manual test with side-by-side screenshots in the viewer.

Cockpits are a special case: they are large hand-painted images with text. The recipe upscales them ×2 the same way, and the mod documents the HD-repaint path (overrides) for anyone who wants hand-made art.

docs.title: The enhanced Lightning: the mesh-patch generator
docs.text:
The X-1A Lightning II (INTTYPEA, 198 faces at LOD 0) is the smallest playable hull and the one seen most, so it is the showcase. Its textures paint raised panels, recessed intakes, vents and a canopy frame on flat faces. A mesh patch is a list of geometric edits addressed by the original face numbers that the viewer shows (W, [ ], I):

# patches/lightning.meshpatch — edits to INTTYPEA LOD 0
# Face numbers come from the model viewer. Units are metres. Texture coordinates of new faces
# are derived from the face they came from, so the original paint lines up with the new shape.

inset    face 41  by 0.12               # intake rim
extrude  face 41  by -0.35              # recess the intake
inset    face 42  by 0.12
extrude  face 42  by -0.35
bevel    edges of faces 10-17 by 0.04   # rounded nose panels
extrude  face 63  by 0.06  taper 0.9    # raised spine panel
cut      face 88  along uv-line (0.31,0.10)-(0.31,0.92) then extrude by -0.02   # panel seam
subdivide faces 20-27 smooth 0.5        # canopy curvature
relief   face 70  from texture height scale 0.03 grid 8   # vents: displacement from the paint
lod      keep 1-3                        # leave the far LODs as they are
Operation Effect inset face N by d Shrinks a face inwards, creating a ring of new faces (a rim). extrude face N by d [taper t] Moves a face along its normal (negative = into the hull), building side walls. bevel edges of faces … by d Chamfers sharp edges. cut face N along uv-line a-b Splits a face along a line given in texture space, so a painted seam can become a real one. subdivide faces … smooth s Splits faces and moves new vertices towards a smooth surface. relief face N from texture height scale h grid g Displaces a grid of new vertices by the texture's brightness (a height map from the paint). lod keep … Copies other LODs unchanged.

All operations keep the one-sided, counter-clockwise convention and the overlay layers (Stage 1), produce new texture coordinates by interpolation from the source face, and are deterministic. Each is a pure function on the engine's Model type with unit tests on small synthetic meshes (a cube face extruded by −1 gives the expected volume; a cut along a UV line produces two faces whose UVs meet on the line).

The patch file contains no original geometry — only face numbers and distances chosen by the author — so it can be published. Applied to someone else's mesh it simply fails the recipe's check (face count and a checksum of the source mesh are recorded in the recipe):

recipes:
  lightning:
    kind: mesh-patch
    input: original:INTTYPEA
    input_faces: 198                # refuse to patch an unexpected mesh
    patch: patches/lightning.meshpatch
    output: models/inttypea.obj     # = the model override path: replaces the Lightning everywhere

Authoring workflow: open the mesh in the viewer (--model INTTYPEA, W, [ ], I), note face numbers, write the patch, and the viewer reloads it on save (Stage 7 adds patch hot-reload) to show the result next to the original.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
# rules/models.yaml — nothing else changes: the parent campaign's rules all apply
modelsets:
  lightning:
    intact: models/inttypea.obj     # generated by recipes.lightning

Every other model set keeps pointing at the originals, and because the upscaled textures land on the texture override paths, every model in the game picks them up without a rule change.

docs.title: Manual tests (Stage 7)
docs.text:
• Side-by-side viewer screenshots of five textures and the Lightning before/after.
  • The enhanced Lightning at every LOD distance; no cracks, no flipped faces (wireframe and culling), paint aligned with the new geometry.
  • A full mission flown with the remastered campaign; frame time unchanged within 10%.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
OpenInterceptor is a library crate (src/lib.rs, crate openinterceptor) with a thin binary on top (src/main.rs, program openinterceptor). Almost all code lives in the library, so every module can be unit-tested with cargo test. The engine is built in layers: each layer uses only the layers below it.

Status

Updated to the code as built in Stage 1, build 0.2.0 (main 909d687): Newtonian flight, settings and data discovery, per-asset overrides, the extractor, HD/3D cockpits, the asset browser and the macOS app bundle. No specification exists yet, so plan stages are cited instead of requirement IDs.

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
The order is the one written at the top of src/lib.rs:

flowchart TB
    subgraph L7["7 · Application"]
        APP["app<br/>launcher, viewer, asset browser, flight session"]
        CK["check<br/>headless validation"]
        EX["extract<br/>CD → OBJ/PNG/WAV"]
        CLI["cli + settings<br/>options, user data folder"]
    end
    subgraph LM["6½ · Missions"]
        MI["mission<br/>MissionRun: roles, waves, objectives, debrief"]
    end
    subgraph L6["6 · Presentation"]
        R["render<br/>camera, gpu, effects, starfield"]
        H["hud<br/>layout, radar, MFD, draw"]
        AU["audio<br/>SoundBank"]
    end
    subgraph L5["5 · Devices"]
        IN["input<br/>Bindings, gamepad::PadState"]
        PL["platform<br/>Gamepads (macOS shim, Linux js)"]
    end
    subgraph L4["4 · Simulation"]
        S["sim<br/>World, flight, combat, systems, ai, targeting, collision"]
    end
    subgraph L3["3 · Content"]
        C["content<br/>Content, vfs, pack, rules, schema, files,<br/>equipment, behaviour, scenario"]
        SC["script<br/>conditions, actions"]
    end
    subgraph L2["2 · Model"]
        M["model<br/>Model, ModelLod, MaterialGroup"]
    end
    subgraph L1["1 · Formats"]
        F["formats<br/>pe, xmsh, xtxr, tga, wav, ini, yaml, obj"]
    end
    APP --> R & H & AU & IN & S & C & MI
    MI --> S & C & SC
    CK --> S & C & F
    R --> S & C & M
    H --> S
    AU --> S & C
    IN --> S
    PL --> IN
    S --> C & SC
    C --> M & F & SC
    M --> F

sim never calls render, hud, audio or macroquad: it is plain data advanced at a fixed rate, which is what makes it deterministic and unit-testable.

docs.title: Data flow: from the CD to a frame
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    CD[("player's CD<br/>DLLs, INI, WAV")] --> OD["content::vfs::OriginalData<br/>files by name + pe::ResourceFile"]
    PK[("packs/*<br/>pack.yaml, rules, scenarios (YAML), OBJ, PNG")] --> CT["content::Content::load"]
    OD --> CT
    CT --> RU["content::rules::Ruleset"]
    CT --> SC["content::scenario::Scenario"]
    CT --> LD["Content::load_model / load_texture /<br/>load_image / load_sound"]
    LD --> MC["render::gpu::ModelCache<br/>GpuModel (Mesh per texture)"]
    RU --> W["sim::World::from_scenario"]
    SC --> W
    W --> RN["render::Renderer<br/>sky → solid → glow"]
    MC --> RN
    W --> HD["hud::draw<br/>instruments, targeting"]
    RN --> FR["frame"]
    HD --> FR

docs.title: Logic flow: one frame of a flight session
docs.text:
app::flight::FlightSession::frame:

flowchart TD
    A["next_frame().await"] --> B["app::devices::Devices::read → RawInput"]
    B --> C["Bindings::translate → Controls, Vec<Command>, ChaseInput"]
    C --> D["apply commands now<br/>targeting, views, MFD, wing orders, pause"]
    D --> E["player.controls = controls.carry_unconsumed(&previous)"]
    E --> F{"accumulator ≥ TICK (1/60 s)?"}
    F -->|yes| G["World::step()<br/>ai → requests → flight → combat → collisions → systems"]
    G --> H["world.events → Effects::on_events,<br/>SoundBank::play_events, event_messages"]
    H --> F
    F -->|no| I["view_pose → SpaceCamera"]
    I --> J["Renderer: draw_sky, draw_world, draw_glows"]
    J --> K["hud::draw: targeting, cockpit art, instruments"]
    K --> A

docs.title: Event flow
docs.text:
The simulation reports what happened as sim::SimEvent values in world.events (cleared at the start of every World::step). Three consumers read them, none of which can change the simulation:

flowchart LR
    W["World::step"] --> EV["world.events: Vec<SimEvent>"]
    EV --> FX["render::effects::Effects::on_events<br/>explosions, sparks, debris"]
    EV --> SB["audio::event_sound → SoundBank::play"]
    EV --> MS["app::flight::event_messages → hud::MessageLog"]

docs.title: Key Symbols
docs.text: Symbol Where What it is, in plain words main src/main.rs Parses the command line; runs --help/--list/--check without a window, otherwise opens one with macroquad::Window::from_config and runs app::run. Content src/content/mod.rs Everything loaded: packs, the original data, the Ruleset, the scenarios; plus asset loaders. Ruleset src/content/rules.rs Every ship, beam, missile, faction, system and cockpit, plus the flight, power and damage rules, after all packs of the chosen campaign are layered. Model src/model.rs A format-neutral 3D model (from XMSH or OBJ): right-handed, −Z forward, LODs, per-texture triangle groups. World src/sim/mod.rs The battle: ships, bolts, missiles, events. Changed only by World::step. Renderer src/render/mod.rs Owns shaders and GPU caches; draws a World from a SpaceCamera. FlightSession src/app/flight.rs One running scenario: world, camera view, HUD state, accumulator.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text: Each layer's public API is on its own page: Formats, Packs, VFS and rules, Assets and GPU cache, Simulation, Conditions, Missions, Rendering, HUD, Input, Audio, Platform, Testbed. cargo doc --open renders the /// comments of every item.

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text:
• openinterceptor --check [--data <cd>] loads and validates everything without a window and prints each error with the file and section it came from. --list prints packs, playable ships and scenarios.
  • openinterceptor --data <cd> --scenario flight-test --ship lightning --view chase starts a scenario directly, skipping the launcher.
  • OI_DEBUG_KEYS=1 prints the name of every key pressed (the name to use in bindings.yaml).
  • Load problems that do not stop the program (missing texture, bad sound) are printed to standard error as warning: / sound: lines.
  • RUST_BACKTRACE=1 for a panic's stack trace. Panics are bugs: bad data must produce an error.
  • Planned (not built): a developer overlay and a --verbose load trace.

docs.title: Assets and GPU cache
docs.text:
Two steps turn a file into something drawable:

  1. src/model.rs converts an XmshMesh or ObjMesh into the format-neutral Model, once, at load time (pure CPU data, unit-tested).
  2. src/render/gpu.rs splits each LOD into per-texture chunks with u16 indices (split_lod, pure, tested) and uploads them as macroquad Meshes with their textures (ModelCache).

Plan: Stage 1.

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    X["xmsh::XmshMesh<br/>D3D: left-handed, +Z forward"] -->|"Model::from_xmsh<br/>negate Z, reverse winding,<br/>fan-triangulate, group by texture"| M["model::Model"]
    O["obj::ObjMesh + materials"] -->|"Model::from_obj<br/>scale, flip v, face normals"| M
    M -->|"gpu::split_lod"| CH["Chunk<br/>texture, vertices, u16 indices"]
    CH -->|"ModelCache::upload"| G["GpuModel<br/>GpuLod { switch_distance, meshes }"]
    T["Content::load_texture"] --> TX["Texture2D cache"] --> G

Engine coordinates everywhere above the formats layer: right-handed, +Y up, −Z forward, metres. The original models use Direct3D's left-handed system with +Z forward, so from_xmsh negates Z and swaps two indices of every triangle so faces still point outwards (a unit test checks the winding).

Collision shapes come from the same data: Model::collision_lod() (the cheapest LOD) gives triangles for station meshes in app::flight::FlightSession::start.

docs.title: Key Symbols
docs.text: Symbol What it is model::Model name, radius, bounds_min/max, lods: Vec<ModelLod> (never empty), attachments. model::ModelLod switch_distance, vertices: Vec<ModelVertex>, groups: Vec<MaterialGroup>. model::MaterialGroup texture: Option<String> and triangle indices: Vec<u32>. model::Attachment A point and facing from an original manipulator (e.g. engine exhaust). render::gpu::Chunk CPU-side chunk ready to become a Mesh (≤ MAX_CHUNK_VERTICES = 16 000). render::gpu::GpuModel GPU LODs plus the CPU Model (kept for stats and collision). render::gpu::ModelCache (reference, pack) → Option<Rc<GpuModel>> and texture caches; failures recorded in errors.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text:
• Model::from_xmsh(&XmshMesh), Model::from_obj(name, &ObjMesh, scale, &[ObjMaterial]).
  • model.lod_for_distance(d), model.collision_lod(), lod.triangle_count(), lod.triangles() -> impl Iterator<Item = [Vec3; 3]>.
  • gpu::split_lod(&ModelLod) -> Vec<Chunk>.
  • ModelCache::get(&Content, reference, pack, scale) -> Option<Rc<GpuModel>>; GpuModel::lod(distance).

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text:
• The model viewer (launcher → Model viewer) shows each model's LOD triangle counts and switch distances, forces a LOD with L, and draws attachment points as RGB axes.
  • A model drawn inside-out or mirrored points at the handedness conversion; a model that is missing shows "could not load" with the ModelCache error underneath.
  • Textures that fail to load leave the group white (macroquad's default texture).

docs.title: Audio
docs.text: src/audio.rs: sound effects driven by simulation events. Plan: Stage 1 (event sounds); music loops and CD audio are Stage 5.

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    R["Ruleset: sounds, beam sound, missile sound"] --> L["SoundBank::load (async)<br/>Content::load_sound → wav::decode (PCM / MS ADPCM / IMA ADPCM)<br/>→ Pcm::to_wav_bytes → load_sound_from_bytes"]
    EV["world.events"] --> ES["event_sound(world, event, listener, ear)<br/>→ (SoundKey, volume)"]
    ES --> P["SoundBank::play"]
    L --> P

event_sound is pure and tested: beam and missile sounds use the firing ship's weapon; hits use shield_hit or hull_hit; destruction uses big_explosion for objects with radius over 100 m, else explosion (always at least 15 % volume); lock and denied only for the listener; since Stage 2, system_damage when one of the listener's systems is damaged (SystemChanged, not repairs), tractor / cloak / ecm when a switchable system goes on or off (Switched; quieter when switching off, attenuated for other ships) and hyperspace when a ship jumps out (Departed), point_defence for each point-defence shot (PointDefence, at 40 % of the distance volume); a destruction whose model set's destroyed_effect, or a missile blast whose explosion effect, has a sound plays that sound instead of the usual event; everything else is attenuated by distance (attenuate: full within 50 m, half at about 350 m).

Cue table (Stage 2, item 2.12). Sound references are resolved when the rules load (rules::build_at): a reference written cue:<Name> is looked up in the table named by audio.cue_table — original:<file>/<section> of an original INI file, the original game's soundfx.ini — whose entry's file name becomes original:<file>.wav. By the time SoundBank loads, every reference is an ordinary asset, so cues need no run-time code. Unknown cues and a missing table are load errors.

Playback uses macroquad's audio feature (quad-snd: CoreAudio on macOS, ALSA on Linux).

docs.title: Key Symbols
docs.text: Symbol What it is SoundKey Named(&'static str), Beam(u16), Missile(u16). NAMED The sixteen event names: explosion, big_explosion, shield_hit, hull_hit, lock, missile_launch, afterburner, target, denied, collision, and since Stage 2 system_damage, tractor, cloak, ecm, hyperspace, point_defence. SoundKey::Effect(i) The sound of effect i (an event name from sounds: or an asset in the effect's pack), loaded with the bank. SoundBank Decoded sounds by key, and errors for sounds that failed.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text:
• SoundBank::load(&Content).await, bank.play(&SoundKey, volume), bank.play_events(&World, listener, ear).
  • event_sound(&World, &SimEvent, ShipId, Vec3) -> Option<(SoundKey, f32)>, attenuate(distance).

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text:
• Sounds that fail to load are printed at start-up as sound: … lines; --check loads every referenced sound too.
  • No sound at all on Linux: the build needs the ALSA development package (libasound2-dev).
  • A cue: sound that is silent: --check names unknown cues (sounds.x: unknown sound cue 'Y'); if the cue resolves, the asset browser shows whether the original file (or its override) loads.

docs.title: Extractor (--extract)
docs.text: src/extract.rs: converts the player's original data into formats every tool edits, writing each file at its override path so an edited copy dropped into a mod replaces the original. Plan: Stage 1 (first version); Stage 6 polishes the modding toolkit.

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    CD["OriginalData<br/>(the player's CD)"] --> M["XMSH → Model::from_xmsh → model_to_obj<br/>models/<name>.obj + .mtl"]
    CD --> T["XTXR → RGBA → png()<br/>textures/<name>.png"]
    CD --> I["TARG (TGA, incl. colour-mapped) → RGBA<br/>cockpit cyan → alpha → png()<br/>images/<dll>/<id>.png"]
    CD --> S["*.wav (MS/IMA ADPCM, PCM) → Pcm → to_wav_bytes<br/>sounds/<name>.wav"]
    CD --> R["*.ini, *.txt copied<br/>original-data/"]
    M & T & I & S & R --> OUT["<DIR>/ with pack.yaml (interceptor-extracted) and README.txt"]
  • Models: the most detailed LOD, in the engine's convention (metres, +Y up, nose along −Z), so positions are written unchanged; texture v is flipped back (1 − v) because Model::from_obj flips it on load — a round trip is exact (unit-tested). Textured groups get map_Kd ../textures/<tex>.png; untextured faces become flat_rrggbb materials with a Kd colour. Materials are kept in a BTreeMap so the output is identical run to run.
  • Images: the original cockpits mark see-through areas with cyan (0x03DF); for cockpit DLLs that becomes alpha 0. Sprites and menu art use colour-mapped TGA, also decoded.
  • On the full CD: 297 models, 799 textures, 3244 images, 792 sounds, 27 reference files, 0 errors, about 2.4 s and 195 MB.

The output is the player's own copy of copyrighted content: personal modding only, never to be shared or committed. The README written into the folder says so.

docs.title: Key Symbols
docs.text: Symbol What it is ExtractReport Counts per kind plus error messages; summary(). model_to_obj(&Model, name) -> (obj, mtl) OBJ + MTL text for LOD 0. png(&Image) -> Result<Vec<u8>, String> PNG encoding via the image crate. pack_files() -> (pack.yaml, README) The texts written at the top of the folder.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text:
• extract::run(&Content, out: &Path) -> Result<ExtractReport, String> — errors if no original data is loaded; individual asset failures go into the report.
  • CLI: openinterceptor --extract <DIR> (exits 1 if any asset failed).

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text:
• Each failure names the asset (image spritesdll.dll#28771: …). The extractor shares every reader with the game, so a failure here is also a failure in play — fix the reader, add a unit test with a synthetic file.
  • To check an override end to end, copy one extracted file into a mod at the same relative path and open the launcher's Asset browser: it shows [overridden by <mod>].

docs.title: Formats layer
docs.text: src/formats/: turns bytes into plain Rust data. Nothing here knows about windows, GPUs, rules or the simulation, so every reader is tested with small byte buffers built inside the test itself — never with original game files. Plan: Stage 1 (formats needed for flight).

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    B["&[u8]<br/>borrowed bytes"] --> RD["Reader<'a><br/>bounds-checked little-endian reads"]
    RD --> PE["pe::ResourceFile"]
    RD --> XM["xmsh::parse → XmshMesh"]
    RD --> XT["xtxr::parse → XTexture"]
    RD --> TG["tga::decode → Image"]
    RD --> WV["wav::decode → Pcm"]
    TXT["&str"] --> INI["ini::Ini::parse<br/>(original INI; legacy settings)"]
    TXT --> YML["yaml::parse → Node<br/>(mod files, settings, bindings)"]
    TXT --> OBJ["obj::parse → ObjMesh<br/>obj::parse_mtl"]

Logic flow of a typical reader: check the signature (BadMagic if wrong) → read the header with Reader (every read returns FResult, so ? propagates a Truncated error) → read the tables the header points to → validate cross-references (edge and vertex indices, palette indices) → return owned data.

Module Reads Notes formats::pe Win32 resource tables in the original DLLs Names are stored with quotes ("INTTYPEA"); ResId::name strips and upper-cases them. formats::xmsh XMSH meshes LODs, signed edge references, BSP walked with an explicit stack and a node budget. formats::xtxr XTXR palettised textures Palette 0 (full brightness) of 16 RGB555 shade palettes; top mip only. formats::tga TGA (16/24/32-bit, raw or RLE) Optional colour key (cockpit cyan 0x03DF) → transparent black. formats::wav RIFF WAVE: PCM 8/16, MS ADPCM, IMA ADPCM Re-encodes to PCM WAV in memory for playback. formats::ini INI text Case-insensitive sections/keys, ; comments, layered merge. Since Stage 2 used for the original CD's INI files (inherit: original:…) and to migrate old settings.ini / bindings.ini; mod files are YAML. formats::yaml A strict subset of YAML Block and flow mappings and sequences, plain/quoted scalars, | and > block text, # comments. Rejects tabs, anchors, aliases, tags, several documents, complex keys and multi-line plain scalars with a line number. Every scalar stays text (with a quoted flag); the schema layer gives it a type. Also writes YAML (to_yaml). Why hand-written: DEV-030. formats::obj Wavefront OBJ + MTL The mod model format. Negative indices, v/vt/vn forms. Faces in a g/o named slot_<name> are not kept as geometry: each such group becomes an attachment point (name, centre of its faces, first face's normal) in ObjMesh::slots.

docs.title: Key Symbols
docs.text: Symbol What it is Reader<'a> A borrowed view of bytes with checked u16/i16/u32/i32/f32/name reads. The lifetime 'a ties it to the buffer, so it can never outlive the data. FormatError Why decoding failed: Truncated { offset, wanted, len }, BadMagic { expected }, Invalid(String), Unsupported(String). Implements Display and std::error::Error. FResult<T> Short for Result<T, FormatError>. pe::ResourceFile Owns a DLL's bytes and its resource index; find(kind, id) returns a borrowed slice. pe::ResId Num(u32) or Name(String) — a resource id. xmsh::XmshMesh, Lod, Polygon, XVertex, Manipulator The mesh exactly as stored (Direct3D coordinates). Polygons store a first/count range into one shared polygon_vertices vector. xtxr::XTexture Width, height, palette 0 and the top mip's indices; to_rgba(). tga::Image RGBA, rows top to bottom (also used as content::Image). wav::Pcm Interleaved i16 samples; to_wav_bytes(), duration(). ini::Ini, ini::Section Parsed INI; get, get_f32, get_bool, get_floats, merge_from. yaml::Node, yaml::Value, yaml::YamlError A YAML value with its 1-based line: Null, Scalar { text, quoted }, Seq, Map (entries in file order); an error with line and message. obj::ObjMesh, obj::ObjMaterial Positions, uvs, normals, faces (as corner ranges), material names, slots (attachment points).

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text:
• Reader::new(&[u8]), .u16/.i16/.u32/.i32/.f32(offset), .bytes(offset, n), .name(offset, n).
  • pe::ResourceFile::parse(Vec<u8>), ::open(&Path), .find(&ResId, &ResId) -> Option<&[u8]>, .entries(), .names_of(&ResId).
  • xmsh::parse(&[u8]) -> FResult<XmshMesh>; Lod::polygon_indices(&Polygon) -> &[u32].
  • xtxr::parse(&[u8]) -> FResult<XTexture>; xtxr::rgb555(u16) -> [u8; 3].
  • tga::decode(&[u8], key: Option<u16>) -> FResult<Image>; tga::COCKPIT_KEY_555.
  • wav::decode(&[u8]) -> FResult<Pcm>.
  • Ini::parse(&str), Ini::parse_bytes(&[u8]) (UTF-8 or Latin-1), Ini::parse_with_warnings, ini.section(name), ini.get(section, key), ini.merge_from(&other).
  • obj::parse(&str) -> FResult<ObjMesh>, obj::parse_mtl(&str) -> Vec<ObjMaterial>.

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text:
• openinterceptor --check --data <cd> parses every original mesh and texture and reports each failure by resource name (1 096 resources, 0 errors on the reference CD).
  • A Truncated error names the offset and size requested: compare with the byte tables on the format pages.
  • To inspect a resource by hand, the format pages describe the layout field by field; the build_test_* helpers show the same layout as code.
  • A YAML problem reads line N: message (callers add the file name). The reader works line by line: a block parser for indentation (BlockParser) and a small flow parser for […] and {…}, which may wrap over several lines inside the brackets.

docs.title: Cockpit and HUD
docs.text: src/hud/: the 2D layer over the 3D view. hud/mod.rs holds the pure logic (tested); hud/draw.rs paints it with macroquad (verified by manual tests). hud/layout.rs holds the pure maths of 3D-cockpit anchors and the cockpit layout editor. Plan: Stage 1; Stage 2 added the power and systems instruments, status flags, the MFD Systems page, text fitted to each instrument, instruments anchored in perspective on a 3D cockpit and the layout editor (F12).

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    W["World + player ShipId"] --> L["pure logic<br/>radar_point, gauge_values, gauge_angle,<br/>mfd_lines, MessageLog::visible,<br/>power_readout, system_lamps, status_flags"]
    CK["CockpitDef.instruments + design<br/>(or default_instruments, 640×480)"] --> LY["Layout::new(screen, design)<br/>design space → pixels"]
    L --> D["draw::draw_targeting<br/>draw::draw_cockpit<br/>draw::draw_instruments<br/>(skips anchored ones)"]
    LY --> D
    AN["CockpitDef.anchors"] --> AC["layout::anchor_corners<br/>(+ model_offset)"]
    AC --> DA["app::flight::draw_anchored<br/>draw_instrument → RenderTarget<br/>→ grid mapped onto the corners"]
    L --> DA

Anchored instruments (3D cockpits). An anchor (at, normal, size, metres from the eye) is a rectangle lying on the cockpit model's surface. anchor_corners builds its four corners: "up" is world +Y with its component along the normal removed (Gram–Schmidt), "right" completes the frame. Each frame, draw_anchored (in app::flight) projects the corners to measure the instrument's on-screen footprint, draws the instrument with draw::draw_instrument into a RenderTarget at about twice that size (so lines stay sharp), and maps the texture onto the rectangle through a grid of small quads (anchor_point interpolates the corners), because one quad of two triangles would bend straight lines at its diagonal. The instrument then sits in its bezel at any window shape and field of view. HudFrame::anchored names the instruments drawn this way, and draw_instruments skips them.

Text fitted to instruments. Every instrument painter sizes its text to its box (fit_size: the longest line, measured once at a reference size, scaled to fit the width and the row count to fit the height, capped at a maximum). The MFD uses one size for every page, fitted to the longest page, so text does not jump when pages change. Lines and text also scale with an anchored instrument's texture.

Design space. Instruments are placed in a cockpit's design space (instruments: {mfd: [x, y, w, h]} in the rules). The original cockpits use 640×480, the default; a cockpit can declare its own with design: [w, h] (the default campaign's Guard cockpit uses 1280×720). Layout::new(screen, design) scales the design space as large as fits (min(screen.w / design.w, screen.h / design.h)) and centres it: a 4:3 cockpit fills the height of a 16:9 screen with space visible at the sides; a 16:9 design fills it exactly. The cockpit image is stretched to the whole design space (Layout::full), whatever its pixel size — which is why an HD repaint (e.g. 2560×1920 replacing a 640×480 original) keeps every instrument aligned without changing a rule.

Instruments (names used in cockpit rules):

Name Shows radar_front, radar_rear Contacts in the front / rear hemisphere; distance from the centre = angle off the axis (rim = 90°); rear scope mirrored left/right. Faction colours; stations drawn larger; the target boxed. Mobile contacts beyond [flight] RadarRange are hidden. mfd One of five pages (MfdPage): Target (name, faction, range, speed, shields, armour, hull, lock state), Weapons (beams, link mode, racks with the selected one marked >), Status (own shields with balance, armour/hull/energy, and the power line BEAM x SHLD y PWR used/budget), Systems (one line per fitted system: OK, ON, DMG n%, OUT, DESTROYED, * while being repaired), Nav. gauge1–gauge4 Needles for speed, energy, shields, hull (red below 25 %). message The newest message younger than 4 s. power B-<level> and S-<level> columns (charge settings), fore/aft shield bars with the favoured facing marked, used/budget in yellow when the budget is full (power_readout). systems A grid of lamps, one per fitted system with a three-letter label (system_abbrev): green OK, cyan switched on, amber damaged, red knocked out (blinking while repaired), grey destroyed (system_lamps, Lamp).

Fallback panels. A cockpit that does not place power or systems gets them as small panels at the top right of its own design space — x from 87.5 % of the design width, y from 9 % of its height — with a dark backdrop over cockpit art. The glass layout (default_instruments) places both along the bottom.

Ships without cockpit art, and the non-cockpit views, use glass instruments (default_instruments() with dark backgrounds). A throttle/speed/REV/BURN/VCT strip is drawn under the message line, extended with BRAKE while braking and HOLD n while the flight computer holds a speed, and the Stage 2 status flags (status_flags): DISABLED, CLOAKED, TRACTOR, ECM, JUMP n (hyperspace countdown).

Targeting (forward views): a reticle; corner brackets sized by the target's angular size; name and range; a lead circle (where to aim beams); a lock-progress ring, then a red lock diamond and LOCK; an arrow on a ring when the target is off-screen. Nav points draw a blue diamond.

MfdPage, mfd_lines(&World, ShipId, page, nav) -> Vec<String> MFD content. MessageLog Timestamped messages; push, visible(now, n); bounded to 32.
