docs.title: Learn Rust with this codebase
docs.text:
This section teaches the Rust you need to fully understand OpenInterceptor, using examples from its own modules. It assumes you can program in another language (C, C++, C#, Python, Java…) but not that you know Rust.

Read in order; each page builds on the previous one.

Page You will be able to read… Ownership and borrowing Who owns the World, the meshes, the textures; why & and &mut matter; interior mutability with Cell (ObjectContext) Lifetimes and borrowed bytes The format readers, which parse a DLL without copying it; naming lifetimes on a returned iterator (rules::of) Structs, enums and pattern matching Ship, Action, View, FormatError and every match; enum decisions (Tow); const fn tables (ACTIONS); recursive enums and a recursive-descent parser (script::Expr) Traits and generics Default, Debug, From, Iterator, macroquad's Camera Error handling Result, ?, per-layer error enums; why bad data never panics Modules and visibility The src/ tree, mod, pub, pub(crate) Iterators and closures Rule merging, polygon triangulation, target selection; returning impl Iterator (pack::needs) Collections Vec, HashMap, when to use which FFI, repr(C) and unsafe The macOS gamepad shim Platforms with cfg macOS / Linux / other code paths Testing in Rust #[test], #[cfg(test)], unit vs integration tests Cargo Cargo.toml, profiles, Cargo.lock, pinned versions, build.rs Async and the macroquad loop macroquad::Window::from_config, next_frame().await, the fixed-timestep accumulator

Further reading: The Rust Programming Language (the "Book", free at doc.rust-lang.org/book) covers each topic in depth; Rust by Example has runnable snippets.

docs.title: Async and the macroquad loop
docs.text: A game draws a frame, waits for the display, and repeats. macroquad expresses that wait with Rust's async/await, so the loop reads like straight-line code.

docs.title: Starting the window only when needed — src/main.rs
docs.text:
Many macroquad programs use the #[macroquad::main] attribute, which opens the window before main runs. OpenInterceptor has modes that must not open a window (--help, --list, --check), so it uses a plain main and creates the window explicitly:

fn main() {
    let options = cli::parse(&args, std::env::var("OPENINTERCEPTOR_DATA").ok())?;
    if let Some(code) = headless(&options) {       // --help, --list, --check
        std::process::exit(code);
    }
    let conf = window_conf(options.fullscreen);
    macroquad::Window::from_config(conf, app::run(options));   // runs the async app
}

docs.title: The loop — src/app/mod.rs
docs.text:
pub async fn run(options: Options) {
    let content = Content::load(&options.content_config())?;   // (error screen on failure)
    let renderer = Renderer::new()?;
    let sounds = SoundBank::load(&content).await;               // macroquad's loader is async
    let mut ctx = AppContext { content, renderer, sounds, … };
    let mut screen = Screen::Launcher(launcher::Launcher::new(&ctx));
    loop {
        let next = match &mut screen { … => s.frame(&mut ctx) };  // input, sim, draw
        // switch screens according to `next` …
        next_frame().await;                                      // wait for the next frame
    }
}

docs.title: What async and .await mean here
docs.text: An async fn returns a future: a computation that can pause. .await pauses it until the awaited thing is ready. macroquad runs our run future on its own tiny executor, resuming it once per frame. There are no threads involved and no async runtime such as Tokio.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Anything that waits for a frame must be async and .awaited. In this codebase that is app::run, SoundBank::load, and the asset browser's AssetBrowser::frame, which loads a sound for playback with macroquad's async fn load_sound_from_bytes. Making that one screen method async costs nothing: the app loop is already async and simply writes Screen::Assets(a) => a.frame(&mut ctx).await.
  • A tempting shortcut — a hand-made block_on that polls the future in a loop — was rejected when writing the asset browser: it needs an unsafe waker (or Waker::noop) and spins forever if the future is ever Pending. .await inside the async loop is both safe and simpler.
  • Screen frame functions and World::step are ordinary functions called from the loop, which keeps them testable without a window.

docs.title: Fixed timestep inside a variable frame rate — src/app/flight.rs
docs.text:
let dt = get_frame_time().min(MAX_FRAME);   // cap stalls at 0.25 s
self.accumulator += dt;
while self.accumulator >= TICK {            // TICK = 1/60 s
    self.world.step();
    // … effects, sounds and messages from this tick's events
    self.accumulator -= TICK;
}

The display may run at 60, 120 or 144 Hz; the simulation always advances in 1/60 s steps, so behaviour does not depend on the machine. A side effect worth knowing: at 120 Hz about half the frames run no tick, so a key press seen in such a frame must be kept until a tick consumes it — that is Controls::carry_unconsumed in src/sim/mod.rs. See Architectural design.

docs.title: Cargo
docs.text: Cargo builds the project, fetches dependencies and runs tests.

docs.title: Cargo.toml
docs.text:
[package]
name = "openinterceptor"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"          # language edition
rust-version = "1.86"     # oldest compiler supported

[dependencies]
macroquad = { version = "=0.4.14", features = ["audio"] }   # "=" pins this exact version
glam = "=0.27.0"                                            # maths (already in macroquad's tree)
image = { version = "=0.24.9", default-features = false, features = ["png"] }

[profile.dev]
opt-level = 1             # debug builds still fast enough to fly

[profile.release]
lto = "thin"              # link-time optimisation for release builds

docs.title: Pinned versions and Cargo.lock
docs.text: "=0.4.14" accepts only that version; plain "0.4.14" would accept any compatible 0.4.x. We pin exactly because an upgrade is a decision (dependency policy). Cargo.lock records the exact version of every transitive dependency; it is committed, so every build of a given commit uses the same code.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text: Command Profile Use cargo build / cargo run dev Fast compile, debug checks (integer overflow panics) cargo build --release release Optimised; what testers run cargo test test (dev settings) Unit tests

docs.title: Features
docs.text: Optional parts of a crate, switched on in Cargo.toml. macroquad 0.4.14 does not enable sound by default, so we turn on its audio feature (it logs "audio feature disabled" if you forget). For image we do the opposite: default-features = false and only png, so no other decoders are compiled.

docs.title: build.rs
docs.text: A program Cargo runs before compiling the crate. Ours compiles the macOS gamepad shim and tells Cargo which frameworks to link (cargo:rustc-link-lib=framework=GameController).

docs.title: Library and binary
docs.text: src/lib.rs makes the package a library crate named openinterceptor; src/main.rs is the binary of the same name, which uses the library like any other crate would. cargo test runs the library's tests.

docs.title: Everyday commands
docs.text: cargo check (type-check only, fastest), cargo clippy (lints), cargo fmt (formatting), cargo doc --open (browse the /// docs of the whole crate).

docs.title: Platforms with cfg
docs.text: #[cfg(...)] includes code only when a condition holds at compile time. Code for another OS is not compiled at all — not just skipped at run time.

docs.title: src/platform/mod.rs
docs.text:
#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]
mod linux;
#[cfg(target_os = "macos")]
mod macos;

#[derive(Default)]
pub struct Gamepads {
    #[cfg(target_os = "linux")]
    linux: linux::JoystickReader,   // this field only exists in Linux builds
}

impl Gamepads {
    pub fn poll(&mut self) -> Option<PadState> {
        #[cfg(target_os = "macos")]
        {
            macos::pad_state(0)
        }
        #[cfg(target_os = "linux")]
        {
            self.linux.poll()
        }
        #[cfg(not(any(target_os = "macos", target_os = "linux")))]
        {
            None
        }
    }
}

Every caller writes gamepads.poll() and never sees cfg. Notice that even a struct field can be conditional: on macOS, Gamepads is an empty struct.

docs.title: cfg! in ordinary code — src/cli.rs
docs.text:
cfg!(…) is a macro that evaluates to true/false; both branches are still compiled:

if cfg!(target_os = "macos") {
    Some(home.join("Library/Application Support/OpenInterceptor"))
} else {
    Some(base.join("openinterceptor"))
}

docs.title: In build.rs
docs.text:
A build script runs on the build machine, so it checks the target with environment variables:

if std::env::var("CARGO_CFG_TARGET_OS").as_deref() == Ok("macos") {
    macos_shim(); // xcrun clang … oi_platform.m; link GameController and Foundation
}

docs.title: Checking another platform's code
docs.text: cargo check --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu type-checks the Linux paths from a Mac (after rustup target add x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu) without building or running them.

docs.title: cfg(test)
docs.text: #[cfg(test)] code exists only in test builds — see Testing.

docs.title: Collections
docs.text: Type Use it for In this codebase Vec<T> An ordered, growable array. The default choice. Vertices, polygons, ships, bolts, stars, rules definitions, INI entries HashMap<K, V> Lookup by key Resources by (type, id) (pe::ResourceFile), original files by name (OriginalData), bindings by Action, the model and texture caches (ModelCache), cockpit instruments by name HashSet<T> "Is this in the set?" Keys held / pressed this frame (RawInput), textures already checked (check::run) [T; N] Fixed-size array A colour [f32; 3], a rectangle [f32; 4], a palette [u16; 256], the four gauge values &[T] A borrowed view into any of the above Function parameters such as &[u8]

docs.title: Rules of thumb
docs.text:
• Default to Vec. It is contiguous in memory, which is what CPUs are fastest at. A linear scan of a few dozen ships beats a HashMap lookup. ini::Section keeps its entries in a Vec<(String, String)> for that reason — sections are small and file order matters.
  • Use a HashMap when you look things up by key many times (resources, caches).
  • Store indices into a Vec (ShipClassId, ShipId) rather than references to its elements, so the Vec can grow and the borrow checker stays out of the way.
  • Take &[T] (not &Vec<T>) as a parameter: it accepts arrays and slices too.
  • Reuse a Vec across frames with clear() instead of creating a new one — clear keeps the allocated memory. Renderer does this for its glow and sky buffers.
  • A bounded log: hud::MessageLog keeps at most 32 entries in a Vec, removing the oldest. (VecDeque would make that removal O(1); at 32 entries a Vec is simpler and fast enough.)

docs.title: Order matters for determinism
docs.text:
HashMap iteration order is random per run. Anything that affects the simulation or what is shown (pack order, rules, scenarios, the launcher list) iterates a Vec that is sorted explicitly — pack::discover sorts folders, files_with_ext sorts file names, scenarios are sorted by order then title, OriginalData::resource_names sorts names.

When the output of a map is written out, a BTreeMap (kept sorted by key) is the simpler choice. The extractor (src/extract.rs, model_to_obj) collects the materials of a model in a BTreeMap<String, String> and writes them with into_values(): the .mtl file is byte-for-byte the same on every run, so extracting twice and comparing — or keeping the files in version control of your own art project — shows only real changes.

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text: Rust has no exceptions. A function that can fail returns Result<T, E>: Ok(value) or Err(error). The caller must deal with it — the compiler warns if a Result is ignored.

docs.title: An error enum — src/formats/mod.rs
docs.text:
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
pub enum FormatError {
    Truncated { offset: usize, wanted: usize, len: usize },
    BadMagic { expected: &'static str },
    Invalid(String),
    Unsupported(String),
}

impl fmt::Display for FormatError { … }        // readable messages for logs and --check
impl std::error::Error for FormatError {}

pub type FResult<T> = Result<T, FormatError>;  // a short alias

docs.title: The ? operator — src/formats/xmsh.rs
docs.text:
? means "if this is an error, return it from my function now; otherwise give me the value":

pub fn parse(data: &[u8]) -> FResult<XmshMesh> {
    let r = Reader::new(data);
    if r.bytes(12, 4)? != b"MSH\0" {                  // `?` stops here if the data is too short
        return Err(FormatError::BadMagic { expected: "MSH" });
    }
    let name = r.name(0, 12)?;
    let radius = r.f32(0x20)?;
    …
}

docs.title: Collecting results
docs.text:
collect::<Result<Vec<_>, _>>() turns "a list of results" into "a result of a list": the first error stops the whole thing. From xmsh::parse_lod:

let textures = (0..nt)
    .map(|i| r.name(base + toff + 32 * i, 32))
    .collect::<FResult<Vec<_>>>()?;

docs.title: One error type per layer
docs.text:
The formats layer has FormatError. Higher layers turn it into a message with context, using map_err, so the user sees where it happened — from Content::load_model:

let mesh = xmsh::parse(data).map_err(|e| format!("mesh {name}: {e}"))?;

The content and app layers use Result<T, String>: their errors are only ever shown to people, so a descriptive string is enough (a choice revisited if a caller ever needs to branch on the kind of error).

docs.title: Why bad data never panics
docs.text:
panic! (and unwrap() on a None/Err) stops the program. Mod authors will feed the engine broken files, so every reader validates offsets and counts and returns an error instead. unwrap() / expect() appear only where failure is impossible, with the reason stated:

Ok(u32::from_le_bytes(b.try_into().unwrap()))           // `bytes` returned exactly 4 bytes
self.lods.last().expect("a Model always has at least one LOD")

Panics remain for bugs — a broken invariant of our own code — never for input.

docs.title: Errors you collect, not return
docs.text: Loading a ruleset does not stop at the first mistake: rules::build returns (Ruleset, Vec<String>) — everything that loaded, plus one message per broken definition — so one typo does not stop a whole mod, and --check can list every problem at once.

docs.title: FFI, repr(C) and unsafe
docs.text: macOS reports gamepads through Apple's GameController framework, which is Objective-C. Rust calls it through a tiny Objective-C file (macos/shim/oi_platform.m) compiled by build.rs, using the foreign function interface (FFI).

docs.title: The shared struct: #[repr(C)]
docs.text:
Rust may reorder a struct's fields for efficiency. When C code reads the same memory, the layout must match C's, which #[repr(C)] guarantees:

/// Must match `OiPad` in the shim, field for field.
#[repr(C)]
#[derive(Default)]
struct OiPad {
    buttons: u16, // bitmask in XInput order
    lt: u8,
    rt: u8,
    lx: i16,
    ly: i16,
    rx: i16,
    ry: i16,
}

docs.title: Declaring the C function
docs.text:
extern "C" {
    fn oi_pad_state(index: u32, out: *mut OiPad) -> i32;
}

*mut OiPad is a raw pointer: Rust cannot check what the other side does with it.

docs.title: unsafe: a promise the compiler cannot check
docs.text:
Calling a foreign function is unsafe: the programmer, not the compiler, vouches that the call is correct. We confine it to one small function and explain why it is sound:

pub fn pad_state(index: u32) -> Option<PadState> {
    let mut raw = OiPad::default();
    // SAFETY: `raw` is a valid, writable `OiPad` with the shim's exact C layout
    // (`#[repr(C)]`, same field order and types); the shim writes it only on success and
    // keeps no pointer to it after returning.
    let connected = unsafe { oi_pad_state(index, &mut raw) } == 1;
    connected.then_some(PadState { buttons: raw.buttons, lt: raw.lt, rt: raw.rt, … })
}

docs.title: Our rules for unsafe
docs.text:
1. Only where there is no safe alternative. There are exactly two unsafe blocks:
  2. src/platform/macos.rs — the FFI call above;
  3. src/render/mod.rs, unsafe_gl() — macroquad's get_internal_gl() is marked unsafe because the returned reference must not be held across next_frame().await; we use it immediately to push and pop the model matrix and never keep it.
  4. Each block is as small as possible and has a // SAFETY: comment saying why it is sound.
  5. A safe function wraps it, so callers never write unsafe.

The Linux joystick reader needs no unsafe: it opens /dev/input/js0 non-blocking (OpenOptionsExt::custom_flags) and decodes 8-byte events with from_le_bytes.

docs.title: Compiling the C side — build.rs
docs.text: The Objective-C file is compiled by the build script with the system toolchain (xcrun clang -c -fobjc-arc …, then xcrun ar crs liboi_platform.a), and the script prints cargo:rustc-link-lib=static=oi_platform and cargo:rustc-link-lib=framework=GameController so Cargo links them. No extra crate is needed.

docs.title: Iterators and closures
docs.text: An iterator produces values one at a time; adapters like map and filter build pipelines that compile down to plain loops.

docs.title: Triangles of a model — src/model.rs
docs.text:
pub fn triangles(&self) -> impl Iterator<Item = [Vec3; 3]> + '_ {
    self.groups.iter().flat_map(move |g| {
        g.indices.chunks_exact(3).map(move |t| {
            [
                self.vertices[t[0] as usize].position,
                self.vertices[t[1] as usize].position,
                self.vertices[t[2] as usize].position,
            ]
        })
    })
}

move |t| … is a closure: an anonymous function that can capture variables from where it is written (here self). The collision mesh for a station is just model.collision_lod().triangles().collect().

docs.title: Picking the nearest hostile — src/sim/targeting.rs
docs.text:
pub fn nearest_hostile(w: &World, me: ShipId) -> Option<ShipId> {
    let my_faction = w.get(me)?.faction;
    others(w, me)                       // Vec<(ShipId, distance)>
        .into_iter()
        .filter(|(id, _)| w.rules.hostile(my_faction, w.ships[id.index as usize].faction))
        .min_by(|a, b| a.1.total_cmp(&b.1))
        .map(|(id, _)| id)
}

Compare with a hand-written loop: same speed, but the intent ("hostile, minimum distance") is in the code's shape. total_cmp gives floats a total order (floats have no Ord because of NaN).

docs.title: Returning an iterator: impl Iterator — src/content/pack.rs
docs.text:
A pack must load after its parent and after every pack it depends on. Two places need "the packs this one needs", so it is one small function — and it returns an iterator, not a Vec:

fn needs(p: &PackInfo) -> impl Iterator<Item = &String> {
    p.parent.iter().chain(p.depends.iter())
}

impl Iterator<Item = &String> means "some iterator over &String; the caller need not know which". The real type (a Chain of an Option iterator and a slice iterator) is long and an implementation detail. Option::iter() yields zero or one item, which is how an optional parent and a list of dependencies become one sequence. Nothing is allocated: the callers just loop or ask a question — needs(p).all(|d| out.iter().any(|q| &q.id == d)) ("is every need already placed?").

The returned iterator borrows from p, so it cannot outlive it; with one reference parameter the compiler infers that lifetime (compare triangles above, which spells it + '_).

docs.title: When we use a plain for loop
docs.text: When the loop body mutates several things, has early exits, or is clearer as steps — e.g. World::step, combat::move_bolts, wav::decode_ms_adpcm. Iterators are a tool, not a rule.

docs.title: collect
docs.text: collect() builds a collection from an iterator; the target type decides which: Vec<_>, HashMap<_, _>, String, or even Result<Vec<_>, E> (stops at the first error) — see Error handling.

docs.title: Lifetimes and borrowed bytes
docs.text:
A lifetime is the compiler's name for "how long a reference is valid". Usually it is inferred. You see it written ('a) when a struct holds a reference.

The original resource DLLs are up to 46 MB. Copying every resource out would waste memory, so the readers work on slices that borrow the file's bytes.

docs.title: Reader<'a> — src/formats/mod.rs
docs.text:
/// A bounds-checked little-endian reader over a borrowed byte slice.
#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
pub struct Reader<'a> {
    data: &'a [u8],
}

impl<'a> Reader<'a> {
    pub fn new(data: &'a [u8]) -> Self {
        Reader { data }
    }

    /// Returns `n` bytes starting at `offset`, or a `FormatError::Truncated`.
    pub fn bytes(&self, offset: usize, n: usize) -> FResult<&'a [u8]> {
        let end = offset.checked_add(n).ok_or(/* Truncated … */)?;
        self.data.get(offset..end).ok_or(/* Truncated … */)
    }

    pub fn u32(&self, offset: usize) -> FResult<u32> {
        let b = self.bytes(offset, 4)?;
        Ok(u32::from_le_bytes(b.try_into().unwrap())) // exactly 4 bytes: cannot fail
    }
}

Reader<'a> promises it will never outlive the bytes it reads. If you kept a Reader after dropping the Vec<u8> it came from, the program would not compile. Note that bytes returns &'a [u8] — a slice of the original buffer, not of the Reader — so the result stays valid even after the small Reader value itself is gone. The Reader is Copy (just a pointer and a length), so passing it around is free.

docs.title: Borrowing out of an owner — src/formats/pe.rs
docs.text:
pub struct ResourceFile {
    bytes: Vec<u8>,                // owns the DLL's bytes
    entries: Vec<ResourceEntry>,
    index: HashMap<(ResId, ResId), usize>,
}

impl ResourceFile {
    /// The resource's bytes, borrowed from this file — no copy.
    pub fn find(&self, kind: &ResId, id: &ResId) -> Option<&[u8]> { … }
}

The signature has no explicit lifetime because of elision: with one reference input (&self), the output borrows from it. Written out it is fn find<'s>(&'s self, …) -> Option<&'s [u8]>: "the slice lives as long as the ResourceFile".

docs.title: Owned output
docs.text: The parsed XmshMesh, by contrast, owns its data (Vec<XVertex>, Vec<Polygon> …), so it can outlive the DLL bytes. This is the pattern throughout formats: borrowed input, owned output. It keeps lifetimes inside the readers and out of the rest of the engine.

docs.title: A lifetime on an iterator — src/model.rs
docs.text:
pub fn triangles(&self) -> impl Iterator<Item = [Vec3; 3]> + '_ { … }

'_ says "this iterator borrows from self": you cannot drop or change the ModelLod while iterating its triangles.

docs.title: Naming the lifetimes yourself — src/content/rules.rs
docs.text:
When a returned iterator borrows from two inputs, the compiler cannot guess which one the '_ means, so the lifetime is written out. While building the ruleset, the resolved definitions of one section are needed again and again:

fn of<'a>(
    resolved: &'a [(String, String, Entry)],
    section: &'a str,
) -> impl Iterator<Item = &'a (String, String, Entry)> + 'a {
    resolved.iter().filter(move |(s, _, _)| s == section)
}

'a ties both inputs and the iterator together: the iterator may hold on to the slice and to section (the move closure captures it), so it lives no longer than either. It is a plain nested function rather than a closure because a closure's signature cannot declare a lifetime parameter like this.

docs.title: Modules and visibility
docs.text:
A Rust package can hold a library crate (src/lib.rs) and a binary crate (src/main.rs). OpenInterceptor puts almost everything in the library; the binary only parses the command line and starts the app (use openinterceptor::{app, check, cli, content::Content};). Keeping the code in the library means cargo test can test every module, and other tools can reuse it.

A crate is a tree of modules. pub mod formats; in lib.rs tells the compiler to load src/formats.rs or src/formats/mod.rs:

src/
  lib.rs           pub mod formats; pub mod model; pub mod content; pub mod sim; …
  main.rs          the `openinterceptor` program
  formats/
    mod.rs         pub mod pe; pub mod xmsh; …   + shared Reader, FormatError, FResult
    pe.rs
    xmsh.rs
  sim/
    mod.rs         World, Ship, ShipId, Controls, SimEvent …
    flight.rs  combat.rs  ai.rs  targeting.rs  collision.rs

docs.title: Visibility
docs.text:
Everything is private by default — visible only inside its own module and its children.

Keyword Visible to Example (none) This module and its children fn parse_lod in xmsh.rs pub(super) The parent module — pub(crate) The whole crate pe::build_test_pe (a test helper other modules' tests use) pub Everyone, including other crates (the binary, tools) xmsh::parse

We use pub for a module's intended API and keep helpers private, so a reader can see at a glance what other layers are meant to call.

docs.title: use
docs.text:
use crate::formats::{ini::Ini, obj, tga, wav, xmsh, xtxr};  // from the crate root
use super::{Controls, Ship};                               // from the parent module (sim/flight.rs)

docs.title: Layering rule
docs.text: Modules may only use modules in their own or lower layers: sim never imports render, hud or macroquad. Rust does not enforce this by itself; the order is written at the top of src/lib.rs and checked in review.

docs.title: Ownership and borrowing
docs.text:
Rust has no garbage collector and no manual free. Instead, every value has exactly one owner, and the value is dropped (freed) when its owner goes out of scope.

fn load() {
    let bytes: Vec<u8> = std::fs::read("xobjects1.dll").unwrap(); // `bytes` owns 28 MB
    let table = ResourceTable::parse(&bytes);                       // lends it, no copy
} // `bytes` dropped here: the memory is freed, exactly once

docs.title: Moving
docs.text:
Assigning or passing a value moves it: the old name can no longer be used.

// src/app/flight.rs, FlightSession::start (simplified)
let (world, player) = World::from_scenario(&scenario, rules.clone(), Arc::new(shapes), choice)?;
let session = FlightSession { world, player, … }; // `world` moved into the session
// world.step();  // error: value moved

This is how OpenInterceptor makes ownership obvious: the FlightSession owns its World; the Renderer's ModelCache owns the GPU meshes and textures. Nobody else can free them by accident.

docs.title: Sharing: Arc and Rc
docs.text:
Sometimes several owners really do need the same data. The World and the session share one read-only Ruleset through Arc<Ruleset> (atomically reference-counted): cloning an Arc copies a pointer and bumps a counter; the ruleset is freed when the last owner goes. The model cache hands out Rc<GpuModel> — the cheaper single-threaded version — because rendering happens on one thread.

Small plain values (f32, u32, Vec3, our ShipId) implement Copy, so they are copied instead of moved.

docs.title: Borrowing: & and &mut
docs.text:
Instead of moving, you can borrow:

  • &T — a shared, read-only reference. Any number may exist at once.
  • &mut T — an exclusive, writable reference. Only one may exist, and no &T at the same time.
impl Renderer {
    // Drawing only reads the world; it changes the renderer's own caches and buffers.
    pub fn draw_world(&mut self, content: &Content, world: &World, effects: &Effects,
                      cam: &SpaceCamera, sun: Vec3, hide: Option<ShipId>) { … }
}
impl World {
    // Stepping changes the world.
    pub fn step(&mut self) { … }
}

The signatures tell you, without reading the body, that drawing cannot change the battle. The compiler enforces it: this rule ("one writer or many readers") is what removes data races and many use-after-free bugs at compile time.

docs.title: Interior mutability: Cell — src/sim/ai.rs
docs.text:
The condition language asks a context for values through a trait whose method takes &self:

pub trait Context {
    fn query(&self, id: u16, args: &[f32]) -> Value;
}

Shared access is right for almost every query — reading a ship's hull changes nothing. But random(0.3) must advance the pilot's random-number generator, which is a change. Rather than make every query take &mut self, ObjectContext keeps the generator state in a std::cell::Cell:

pub struct ObjectContext<'a> {
    pub world: &'a World,
    pub me: ShipId,
    pub state_time: f32,
    pub rng: Cell<u64>,         // changeable through &self
}
// inside query(&self, …):
let mut r = self.rng.get();     // copy out
let roll = next_random(&mut r);
self.rng.set(r);                // copy back

Cell<T> allows changing a Copy value through a shared reference by only ever copying it in and out — no reference to the inside is ever handed out, so the borrow rules still hold without any run-time check. (RefCell does the same for non-Copy values, checking borrows at run time.) After the transitions have been tested, the AI copies the advanced state back into its own memory with cx.rng.get().

docs.title: A common beginner problem
docs.text:
let ship = &mut world.ships[0];
let target = &world.ships[1];   // error: world.ships is already borrowed mutably

Fixes used in this codebase:

  • Work with indices (ShipId) instead of long-lived references.
  • Copy out the small values you need first (let target_pos = t.position;).
  • Borrow different fields at the same time — allowed, because the compiler can see they do not overlap. combat::fire_beams holds &mut w.ships[i] while pushing into w.bolts.
  • Read first, write later: ai::think computes every decision into a list, then applies it.
  • Hold your own handle: World::step does let rules = self.rules.clone(); (an Arc clone) so it can borrow a ship class from rules while mutably iterating self.ships.

See Data model.

docs.title: Testing in Rust
docs.text: Rust has testing built in. cargo test compiles a test build and runs every function marked #[test] — 146 of them in this project (list: Unit tests).

docs.title: Unit tests: next to the code — src/sim/flight.rs
docs.text:
/// How much of the turn rate remains at `speed` (1 at rest, 0 at `lock_speed`).
pub fn turn_factor(speed: f32, lock_speed: f32) -> f32 {
    if lock_speed <= 0.0 {
        return 1.0;
    }
    (1.0 - speed.abs() / lock_speed).clamp(0.0, 1.0)
}

#[cfg(test)]           // compiled only for `cargo test`
mod tests {
    use super::*;      // the parent module's items, including private ones

    #[test]
    fn helpers() {
        assert_eq!(turn_factor(0.0, 1000.0), 1.0);
        assert_eq!(turn_factor(500.0, 1000.0), 0.5);
        assert_eq!(turn_factor(2000.0, 1000.0), 0.0);
        …
    }
}

Because the test module is a child of the code's module, it can test private helpers too.

docs.title: Testing readers without the game data
docs.text:
Original data cannot be in the repository, so format tests build tiny valid inputs by hand. src/formats/xmsh.rs has a crate-visible builder used by its own tests and by model's:

#[test]
fn signed_edges_give_the_vertex_loop() {
    let m = parse(&quad()).unwrap();        // quad() calls build_test_xmsh(…)
    let lod = &m.lods[0];
    // +1 (0→1) starts at 0, +2 (1→2) at 1, -3 (2←3) at 2, -4 (3←0) at 3.
    assert_eq!(lod.polygon_indices(&lod.polygons[0]), &[0, 1, 2, 3]);
}

Checks against the real data run through openinterceptor --check when the player's data is present (the gate does this).

docs.title: Testing the simulation
docs.text:
sim::test_support (a #[cfg(test)] pub(crate) mod) builds a tiny in-memory ruleset, so any sim test can set up a world in two lines and step it:

let mut w = world();                          // test_support::world()
let f = w.rules.ship_id("fighter").unwrap();
let me = w.spawn(f, FactionId(0), "me", Vec3::ZERO, Quat::IDENTITY, Pilot::External);
w.get_mut(me).unwrap().controls.fire_beams = true;
w.step();
assert_eq!(w.bolts.len(), 2, "linked: both mounts");

Determinism (fixed TICK, seeded random numbers) is what makes these tests reliable.

docs.title: Testing with files
docs.text: When a feature really reads folders (pack discovery, content loading), tests write a small pack into std::env::temp_dir() with a unique name (the process id), run, and delete it.

docs.title: Integration tests
docs.text: Files in a tests/ folder are compiled as separate crates and see only the public API. This project does not need them yet: unit tests plus --check against the real packs cover the pipelines (check::tests::the_default_campaign_passes loads the repository's own packs/).

docs.title: Useful forms
docs.text:
• assert!(cond, "message {x}"), assert_eq!(a, b), assert!((a - b).abs() < 1e-5) for floats.
  • assert!(matches!(result, Err(FormatError::BadMagic { .. }))) to check an enum variant.
  • cargo test proximity runs only tests whose name contains proximity.

docs.title: Traits and generics
docs.text: A trait is a set of methods a type promises to have — like an interface.

docs.title: Traits we implement
docs.text:
// src/formats/mod.rs
impl fmt::Display for FormatError {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        match self {
            FormatError::Truncated { offset, wanted, len } => {
                write!(f, "data truncated: needed {wanted} bytes at offset {offset}, have {len}")
            }
            FormatError::BadMagic { expected } => write!(f, "bad signature, expected {expected}"),
            …
        }
    }
}
impl std::error::Error for FormatError {}

Display is what println!("{err}") and err.to_string() use; Debug (usually derived) is {err:?}. Most traits here are derived (Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, Default); Default is written by hand only when the default is not "all zeros", as for Bindings (its default is the original key layout) and ChaseOrbit.

docs.title: A trait from macroquad: Camera — src/render/camera.rs
docs.text:
macroquad draws with whatever implements its Camera trait. We supply our own:

impl macroquad::camera::Camera for SpaceCamera {
    fn matrix(&self) -> Mat4 { self.view_projection() }
    fn depth_enabled(&self) -> bool { true }
    fn render_pass(&self) -> Option<macroquad::texture::RenderPass> { None }
    fn viewport(&self) -> Option<(i32, i32, i32, i32)> { None }
}

So set_camera(&cam) accepts our camera, and its projection uses our own near/far planes.

docs.title: Generics and impl Trait
docs.text:
A generic function works for any type that meets its trait bounds. In this codebase generics mostly appear as impl Trait in argument or return position:

// src/hud/mod.rs — accept anything that converts into a String
pub fn push(&mut self, now: f64, text: impl Into<String>) { … }

// src/formats/obj.rs — a const generic: N is a number known at compile time
fn floats<const N: usize>(words: &mut SplitWhitespace, line: usize) -> FResult<[f32; N]> { … }

The compiler generates a specialised copy per type used (monomorphisation), so generics cost nothing at run time.

docs.title: Trait objects: dyn Fn
docs.text:
rules::build must look up sections of original INI files, but the rules module should not know where files live. It takes a function as a trait object:

pub type OriginalLookup<'a> = dyn Fn(&str, &str) -> Option<Section> + 'a;
pub fn build(sources: &[RulesSource], original: &OriginalLookup) -> (Ruleset, Vec<String>) { … }

Content::load passes a closure reading the player's CD; the tests pass one that reads an in-memory string.

docs.title: When we avoid traits
docs.text: Engine code prefers plain structs and enums over trait objects (Box<dyn Trait>). AI behaviours are an enum Behaviour { Idle, Target, Wingman, Enemy } and the app's screens an enum Screen { Launcher(..), Viewer(..), Flight(..) }: easier to read and to match than a hierarchy of objects, and no heap allocation for dynamic dispatch.

docs.title: Structs: plain data — src/sim/mod.rs
docs.text:
/// What a pilot (human or AI) wants the ship to do this tick.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, Default, PartialEq)]
pub struct Controls {
    pub pitch: f32,                 // +1 = nose up
    pub yaw: f32,                   // +1 = nose right
    pub roll: f32,                  // +1 = roll right
    pub slide: Vec2,                // VCT: x right, y up
    pub throttle_set: Option<f32>,  // set the throttle this tick
    pub throttle_delta: f32,
    pub afterburner: bool,
    pub fire_beams: bool,
    pub fire_missile: bool,         // one-shot
    …
}

#[derive(...)] asks the compiler to write common trait implementations: copying (Clone, Copy), printing with {:?} (Debug), comparing (PartialEq), a default value (Default). Plain data with public fields, built with struct literals and ..Default::default():

Controls { yaw: 0.12, throttle_set: Some(0.35), ..Default::default() }   // sim/ai.rs, a practice target

docs.title: Enums: one of several things
docs.text:
Rust enums can carry data in each variant — like a tagged union, but safe.

// src/sim/mod.rs
pub enum SimEvent {
    BeamFired { ship: ShipId, position: Vec3 },
    Hit { ship: ShipId, position: Vec3, shield: bool },
    Destroyed { ship: ShipId, position: Vec3, radius: f32 },
    LockAcquired { ship: ShipId },
    Message { ship: ShipId, text: String },
    …
}

// src/content/vfs.rs
pub enum AssetRef {
    PackFile(String),
    Original { file: Option<String>, resource: Option<String> },
}

docs.title: Enums as decisions — src/sim/systems.rs
docs.text:
A tractor beam changes another ship's velocity. Changing ship B while iterating over ship A would need two mutable borrows of world.ships at once, which Rust refuses. So the update runs in two phases: first read the world and record each decision as a value, then apply them. An enum whose variants carry data is the natural record:

enum Tow {
    /// Drag ship .0 towards velocity .1, changing it by at most .2 m/s².
    Pull(ShipId, glam::Vec3, f32),
    /// The beam of ship .0 lost its hold and switches off.
    Release(ShipId),
}

// Phase 1 (shared borrows only): tows.push(Tow::Pull(target, wanted, pull)) …
// Phase 2 (one mutable borrow at a time):
for tow in tows {
    match tow {
        Tow::Pull(t, wanted, pull) => { /* change ship t's velocity */ }
        Tow::Release(captor) => { /* switch captor's beam off */ }
    }
}

The same pattern drives ai::think. As a bonus, the result no longer depends on the order the ships are visited.

docs.title: Tables built at compile time: const fn — src/input/mod.rs
docs.text:
Every bindable action is one row of a const table: its bindings.yaml name, default keys and pad buttons, menu group and label. The rows are built by a small constructor marked const fn, which the compiler may run while compiling, so the whole table is a constant baked into the program — no start-up code, no allocation:

const fn a(name: &'static str, action: Action, keys: &'static str, pad: &'static str,
           group: Group, label: &'static str) -> ActionInfo {
    ActionInfo { name, action, keys, pad, group, label }
}

pub const ACTIONS: &[ActionInfo] = &[
    a("hyperspace", A::Hyperspace, "H", "LeftShoulder+A", G::Power, "Hyperspace out / abort"),
    …
];

&'static str fields fit because string literals live for the whole program. One table feeds parsing, defaults, the controls menu and the docs, so they cannot disagree.

docs.title: Recursive enums and recursive descent — src/script/mod.rs
docs.text:
A parsed condition such as hull < 25% and not disabled is a tree. An enum can describe a tree if a variant holds more of the same enum — but a value cannot contain itself directly (its size would be infinite), so the children are put on the heap with Box:

pub enum Expr {
    Num(f32),
    Bool(bool),
    Query(u16, Vec<Expr>),          // a Vec is already on the heap
    Not(Box<Expr>),
    Binary(Op, Box<Expr>, Box<Expr>),
    …
}

The parser that builds it is recursive descent: one method per precedence level, each calling the next-tighter level for its operands. Lower levels bind tighter, so a or b and c parses as a or (b and c) with no precedence table:

fn or(&mut self) -> Result<(Expr, Type), String> {
    let (mut e, mut t) = self.and()?;               // the tighter level first
    while self.eat_word("or") {
        let (r, rt) = self.and()?;
        Self::want(Type::Bool, t, "'or'")?;          // type check while parsing
        Self::want(Type::Bool, rt, "'or'")?;
        e = Expr::Binary(Op::Or, Box::new(e), Box::new(r));
        t = Type::Bool;
    }
    Ok((e, t))
}

not calls itself for not not x, and the innermost level (primary) calls back up to or for a bracketed sub-expression — that is the "recursive". Evaluation is a match over the enum that calls eval on the boxed children.

docs.title: match: handle every case — src/app/flight.rs
docs.text:
match view {
    View::Cockpit | View::Forward => (eye, rot),
    View::Left => (eye, look(90.0)),
    View::Right => (eye, look(-90.0)),
    View::RearLeft => (eye, look(135.0)),
    View::RearRight => (eye, look(-135.0)),
    View::Chase => (pos + rot * Vec3::new(0.0, radius * 0.7, radius * 3.2), …),
    View::ChaseManual => { … }
}

match must be exhaustive: add a View::Target variant and every match that forgot it stops compiling. That turns "forgot to handle the new view" from a runtime bug into a build error. Patterns can also test values: SimEvent::LockAcquired { ship } if *ship == player => in event_messages.

docs.title: Option: maybe a value
docs.text:
There is no null. A value that may be absent is Option<T>: Some(x) or None.

pub target: Option<ShipId>,                       // Ship, src/sim/mod.rs

// hud::mfd_lines: `and_then` chains two "maybe" steps
match me.target.and_then(|t| world.get(t)) {
    None => vec!["TARGET".into(), "none".into(), "T next  R nearest".into()],
    Some(t) => { … }
}

Longer chains read like a sentence. The flight session's cockpit setup (FlightSession::start, src/app/flight.rs) loads a 3D cockpit only if the ship has a cockpit, that cockpit has a Model, and the model loads:

let cockpit_model = cockpit_def.and_then(|c| {
    let model = c.model.as_ref()?;          // `?` on an Option: return None early
    let gpu = ctx.renderer.models.get(content, model, c.image_pack, c.model_scale)?;
    Some((gpu, Vec3::from(c.model_offset)))
});
// `filter` keeps a Some only if the condition holds:
let (instruments, design) = match cockpit_def.filter(|_| has_cockpit) {
    Some(c) => (c.instruments.clone(), Vec2::from(c.design)),
    None => (hud::default_instruments(), hud::DESIGN),
};

? works on Option inside a closure or function that returns Option, just as it does on Result — the first None ends the chain.

docs.title: Newtypes
docs.text:
A struct with one field gives a plain number a distinct type:

// src/content/rules.rs
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
pub struct ShipClassId(pub u16);
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
pub struct BeamId(pub u16);

Now a BeamId cannot be passed where a ShipClassId is expected, even though both are u16.

docs.title: A numeric gotcha: f32::signum(0.0) is 1.0
docs.text:
Floats are not integers. 0.0_f32.signum() returns 1.0 (zero is "positive zero"), unlike 0_i32.signum(), which returns 0. The model viewer once used mouse_wheel().1.signum() as the zoom step, so a wheel that had not moved still zoomed in every frame and the camera ran away. The fix is an explicit helper — src/app/viewer.rs:

pub fn wheel_steps(wheel: f32) -> f32 {
    if wheel == 0.0 { 0.0 } else { wheel.signum() }
}

Other float facts this code relies on: NaN != NaN (the gamepad shim checks value != value to detect NaN); min/max/clamp exist on floats but Ord does not, so sorting floats uses total_cmp (collision, targeting).

docs.title: Modding
docs.text:
Modding is the main objective of OpenInterceptor. The engine is a general space-combat simulator toolkit; X-COM: Interceptor is one content pack for it. Everything a game is made of — ships, weapons, stations, cockpits, scenarios, missions, later the tech tree and the campaign — is data in a pack, and packs layer on top of each other.

The most likely use is a custom campaign that uses none of the original assets: your own models, textures, sounds, rules and missions. Such a pack runs with --no-original and can be shared freely, because it contains nothing of MicroProse's.

flowchart LR
    CD[("player's CD<br/>(optional)")] --> I["pack: interceptor<br/>rules + scenarios"]
    S["campaign: default<br/>original-free"]
    M1["mods/my-campaign<br/>(user mods folder)"]
    M2["mods/balance-tweak"]
    I --> L{{"layered ruleset<br/>later packs override earlier"}}
    S --> L
    M1 --> L
    M2 --> L
    L --> E["engine: sim, render, HUD"]

docs.title: What a mod can do
docs.text: Stage You can change 1 Ships (model, cockpit, flight values, mounts, hull/armour/shields, energy), the flight model itself (newtonian or assisted) and arena size, beam weapons, missiles, stations and objects, factions, cockpits (2D art at any resolution, own design space, 3D cockpit models), instrument layout, event sounds, scenarios with any mix of objects and nav points, additional models (OBJ) and textures (PNG/TGA), per-asset replacement of any original model, texture, image or sound 2 (in progress) Done: mod kinds (campaign, addon, library) with parent, targets, format; YAML mod files with schemas (format 2: units, did-you-mean errors, editor completion); ship systems and special equipment (systems, systems+), power sharing (power), damage to systems and repair (damage), capture (capturable), hyperspace time, crippled scenario objects (destroyed_systems, hull), the power and systems instruments; AI behaviours as state machines with the condition language; difficulty levels with per-level values and variants; 3D cockpit instruments anchored in perspective and the F12 layout editor; looks (model sets with damage textures and states, debris sets, effects); missile guidance kinds, damage modes and mines; station modules at attachment points; AI target preferences and systems use (cloak, ECM, power); the sound cue table; point defence; sensor and jamming probes; text keys and translations. To come: XSPT explosions, model-set extras 3 (in progress) Done: missions as data — roles with class lists, counts and arrivals, waves, objectives, optional objectives, timers, outcomes (actions), radio chatter, debriefs. To come: hazards, environments and atmospheric flight, the campaign context, Tier 2 scripts 4 Star map, bases and modules, research tree, manufacturing, economy, enemy strategy 5 Menus, videos, music

docs.title: Two ways to change the game
docs.text:
1. Rules and scenarios — YAML files in a pack. Add new ships, weapons and arenas, or change any value of an existing one by overriding just that key (Rulesets).
  2. Assets — drop a file at an original asset's override path in a pack and it replaces that asset everywhere (Overrides and extraction). openinterceptor --extract <folder> writes every original asset, already converted to OBJ/PNG/WAV, at exactly those paths: extract, edit, copy the edited file into your mod.

The simplest useful mod is one file: a repainted cockpit at modern resolution (walkthrough). Replacing the 2D cockpit with a 3D one is a few lines of rules plus a model (Cockpits).

docs.title: Comparison with XWVM
docs.text:
XWVM plays the original X-Wing from the player's own data, and faces the same problem: 1990s assets by default, modern content when the player wants it. Public sources (a GamingOnLinux article, a Steam discussion, changelog quotes on Mudspike, and the scotsdez/xwvm-sidecars-xwing repository; ModDB refused automated access) describe its approach:

XWVM OpenInterceptor Original assets Read from the player's install; none shipped Same Modern content A separate HD Asset Pack download (new ship models, 3D cockpits, re-recorded music) Any pack or mod Switching Whole packs activated in the launcher's Game Content screen Whole packs switched off in settings.yaml (packs: {disabled: […]}) Granularity Per pack; no documented per-asset override scheme Per asset: a file at the override path replaces one original asset; everything else still comes from the CD Cockpits Legacy VGA cockpit or a 3D cockpit with instruments on in-cockpit screens Original 2D cockpit, HD/widescreen 2D art with its own design space, or a 3D cockpit model with instruments anchored in perspective on its dashboard, placed with the in-game layout editor Missions "Sidecar" XML beside the unmodified original mission Scenario YAML files; rules inherit from original INI sections without editing them Tools No public extractor; community format tools Built-in --extract to OBJ/PNG/WAV at override paths

Both keep original files untouched and never redistribute them. XWVM's lesson on pack activation (toggling a pack had no effect until a restart path was taken) is why our pack list is read once, deterministically, at start-up.

docs.text:

  • Looks: model sets, debris and effects: damage textures, wreck states, debris, explosions.

docs.title: Behaviours and conditions
docs.text: How AI ships fly and fight is data: a behaviour in a pack's behaviours: section, named by a ship class (behaviour: saucer_scout) or by one scenario object (behaviour: … on the object). This is the Tier 1 design of Format: behaviours and scripting, implemented in Stage 2 (src/content/behaviour.rs, src/script/, src/sim/ai.rs).

docs.title: A behaviour
docs.text:
A behaviour is a small state machine. Each state runs one built-in manoeuvre with parameters; transitions move between states when a condition becomes true; skill sets how well the pilot aims and how fast it reacts.

behaviours:
  saucer_raider:
    start: engage
    states:
      engage:
        do: attack
        range: 1.8km
        fire_cone: 3
        burst: {per_level: [0.8s, 1s, 1.2s, 1.5s]}
        pause: {per_level: [1.8s, 1.4s, 1.1s, 0.8s]}
        missiles: {per_level: [0, 14s, 11s, 8s]}      # 0 = no missiles at cadet
      dodge: {do: evade, duration: 2s}
      flee: {do: retreat, jump: true}
    transitions:
      - {from: engage, to: dodge, when: "hit_recently(0.3s) and random(0.25)"}
      - {from: dodge, to: engage, when: "time_in_state > 2s"}
      - {from: "*", to: flee, when: "hull < 20% and difficulty >= ranger"}
    skill:
      aim: {per_level: [0.2, 0.35, 0.5, 0.65]}
      reaction: {per_level: [1.2s, 0.9s, 0.7s, 0.5s]}

ships:
  raider_saucer:
    behaviour: saucer_raider

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> engage
    engage --> dodge: hit_recently(0.3s) and random(0.25)
    dodge --> engage: time_in_state > 2s
    engage --> flee: hull < 20% and difficulty >= ranger
    dodge --> flee: hull < 20% and difficulty >= ranger
  • The ship starts in start (default: the first state listed).
  • Transitions are checked 4 times a second (ai::CHECKS_PER_SECOND), tried in order; the first whose from matches the current state ("*" matches any) and whose condition holds wins. A transition to the state the ship is already in is skipped. time_in_state restarts at 0 on every change.
  • Every condition is parsed and type-checked when the rules load: a misspelt query, a wrong argument or hull and 3 is a load error naming the behaviour, not a surprise in flight.

All keys with types and defaults: Mod file reference › behaviours.

docs.title: Manoeuvres
docs.text: do: What it does Parameters it reads idle Nothing (parked ships, unarmed stations). — circle A slow circle at 35 % of top speed; never shoots (practice targets). — patrol Circles its spawn point. range (radius), speed attack Pursues the target (its current one, else the nearest visible hostile within 8 km) with lead and aim error; fires in bursts inside fire_cone and range (and 95 % of its first beam's reach); launches a missile every missiles seconds when locked; breaks off for 2 s when about to ram; VCT hulls strafe when the target faces them. Without a target it cruises at half speed. range, fire_cone, burst, pause, missiles, speed evade Weaves unpredictably at top speed (VCT hulls also slide). Leave it with a transition on time_in_state. duration retreat Runs from the nearest hostile at top speed, afterburning while energy lasts. jump: true also starts the hyperdrive turret Stays put; beams that can swivel (turret_arc on the ship class) track hostiles within range (and 95 % of the first beam's reach) and fire in bursts. range, burst, pause mine Waits; when a hostile is within range, detonates its first missile rack as an area blast and is gone (Missiles and mines). range (trigger distance) tow Finds the nearest disabled, capturable hostile ship, closes in, tractors it and jumps out with it (tugs; needs a tractor beam fitted). range (search radius, at least 5 km)

docs.title: Using the ship's systems
docs.text:
systems: tells the pilot when to use its ship's equipment and power. Each entry is a condition, checked with the transitions (4 times a second):

behaviours:
  saucer_raider:
    systems:
      cloak: target_distance > 2km          # stay cloaked until 2 km from the target
      ecm: missiles_incoming(3km) > 0       # jam when missiles are coming
      shields_first: hull < 50%             # hurt: favour shields
Key While the condition holds Otherwise cloak The cloak is switched on (if fitted, working and powered). Switched off. ecm ECM on. ECM off. shields_first Power moves one step at a time towards shields (;), up to the top level. — beams_first Power moves towards beams ('), unless shields_first also holds. —

The requests are exactly the player's keys, so the same power budget and fitting rules apply (a ship without a cloak cannot cloak), and firing still drops a cloak. Both campaigns' pilots run ECM against incoming missiles and favour shields when hurt; the raider saucer and the Shade stay cloaked until 2 km from their target.

docs.title: Target preferences
docs.text:
By default an attacker picks the nearest visible hostile (within 8 km for attack, range for turret). prefer: weights that choice: a hostile matching a selector counts as if it were weight times nearer, so {player: 1.5} chases the player over a wingman up to 1.5 times closer. When several selectors match one ship their weights multiply.

behaviours:
  saucer_raider:
    prefer: {player: 1.5}          # go for the player
  station_turret:
    prefer: {fighter: 1.5}         # shoot fighters before freighters and stations
  wraith:
    prefer: {freighter: 3, class:lightning: 1.2}
Selector Matches player The ship the player flies. a ship kind fighter, freighter, capital, drone, station, probe, mine, debris. class:<id> Ships of that class. faction:<id> Ships of that faction.

Weights must be above 0 (below 1 makes a match less attractive). Preferences only apply when the AI picks a new target: it keeps attacking its current one while that stays alive and visible. An unknown selector is a load error ("prefer: 'x' is not player, a ship kind, class: or faction:").

Wingmen keep the role and orders of Simulation › AI; when they engage they fly attack with the parameters and skill of their class's behaviour (its first attack state).

Fallback. An enemy whose class names no behaviour flies the engine's builtin_attack: engage (attack with default parameters) and evade for 2.5 s, entered on hit_recently(0.3s) and random(0.2) and left on time_in_state > 2.5s, with skill aim 0.5, reaction 0.7 s. A pack may define its own builtin_attack to change it.

docs.title: Skill and fire discipline
docs.text:
Setting Effect skill.aim (0 … 1) Every reaction seconds the pilot picks a fresh aim error of up to (1 − aim) × 8° (ai::MAX_AIM_ERROR). At 0.2 the error is up to 6.4°, enough to miss a fighter at a kilometre; at 1 the pilot leads perfectly. skill.reaction Seconds between the pilot's looks at its target: between looks the pilot assumes the target flies straight on from its last sighting, so a slow pilot leads where the target was going. Lead uses the target's velocity relative to the shooter (bolts carry the shooter's velocity). burst, pause Fire for burst seconds, then hold for pause: pilots do not hose a target continuously. fire_cone Only fire when the aim point is within this angle of the nose.

Together with per-level values these make difficulty. Both campaigns ship behaviours for every enemy type in rules/behaviours.yaml — the default campaign's saucers, robots, gun platforms, tugs, hot-rods and Guard pilots; the interceptor Wraith, Spectre, Phantasm, Shade, Harbinger (tow), drones, pirate and corporate pilots and X-COM wingmen (derived from the strategy guide's descriptions; the original's AI is hard-coded). In the default campaign a cadet-level saucer aims within about 6–7°, looks every 1.2–1.4 s and fires short bursts with long pauses; at space ace it aims within about 3°, looks every 0.5 s and fires long bursts.

docs.title: The condition language
docs.text:
Transitions use conditions — small expressions that are true or false:

hull < 25% and not system_damaged(engines)
target_distance < 1.5km or hit_recently(2s)
difficulty >= captain and random(0.3)
Element Written as Numbers 3, 0.25, .5; with a unit straight after: 1.5km, 350m, 2s, 2min, 1h, 1day, 25% (= 0.25) Logic and, or, not, brackets ( … ); and and or stop early (has_target and target_distance < 1km never asks for a distance without a target) Comparisons <, <=, >, >=, ==, != — between numbers, giving true/false Arithmetic +, -, *, /, unary - Constants true, false; the campaign's difficulty level ids stand for their index (captain = 2 in the default campaign) Queries names from the context below, some with arguments: hit_recently(2s)

Precedence, lowest first: or, and, not, comparisons, + -, * /, then numbers, names and brackets. Names are case-insensitive. Types are checked when the rules load: and, or, not and the whole condition need true/false; comparisons and arithmetic need numbers. There is no assignment, loop or user function, so a condition cannot change the game and always finishes; random draws from the pilot's seeded generator, so a battle replays exactly.

docs.title: Object context: what a behaviour can ask
docs.text:
The queries a behaviour's transitions may use, about the ship flying it (src/script/object.rs). Fractions are 0..1 (write 25% or 0.25), distances metres, times seconds.

Query Type Meaning hull number Hull as a fraction of its maximum. shields number Fore + aft shields as a fraction of full. energy number Beam capacitor as a fraction of full. speed number Speed, m/s. has_target true/false The ship has a target. target_distance number Distance to the target, m (very large without one). target_hull number The target's hull fraction (1 without one). target_disabled true/false The target is disabled. target_is_player true/false The target is flown by the player. time_in_state number Seconds since the behaviour entered its state. hit_recently(t) true/false Hit within the last t seconds: hit_recently(2s). random(p) true/false True with probability p per check (seeded): random(0.3). system_damaged(kind) true/false The system is damaged, knocked out or destroyed: system_damaged(engines). kind is one of engines, manoeuvring, sensors, shields, hyperdrive, vct, tractor, cloak, ecm, damage_control. threats(d) number Hostile ships within distance d: threats(2km). allies(d) number Friendly ships within distance d. missiles number Missiles left in all racks. difficulty number The difficulty level's index; compare with level ids: difficulty >= captain. disabled true/false This ship is disabled. towing true/false This ship's tractor beam holds something. missiles_incoming(d) number Hostile missiles homing on this ship within distance d: missiles_incoming(3km). prize_near(d) true/false A disabled, capturable hostile ship is within distance d.

Missions and events (Stage 3) will add their own contexts with the same language.

docs.title: Difficulty
docs.text: Any number in a behaviour may be {per_level: […]}, a behaviour may have variants per level, and conditions can test difficulty — see Rulesets › Difficulty levels. Cloak lock-break chance by difficulty (Stage 2 item 2.7) is still a fixed strength per system.

docs.title: Errors you may see
docs.text: Message (in --check or on the launcher) Cause states.x: say what it does (do: attack, …) A state without do:. states.x: unknown manoeuvre 'y' do: is not one of the nine manoeuvres. start: no state 'b' / transitions[2]: no state 'b' A name that is not a state. unknown name 'hul' … A query or constant that the object context does not have. 'hull' is a number, not a condition (compare it: 'hull > 0') The condition is not true/false. variants: unknown difficulty level 'x' A level id the campaign does not define.

docs.title: Campaigns (design)
docs.text:
Campaigns — the star map, factions and relations, economy, research, bases, pilots, the story and the rival's plan — are designed in full in Game design and mod format:

  • Mod structure: campaign, addon and library mods; parent.
  • Campaign and game flow: start state, difficulty, arcs, rival plans, score, endings.
  • Strategy layer: map, relations, economy, research, bases, ships, pilots, strategist.
  • Missions, environments and events.

They are implemented in Stages 4 and 5 (plan). The default campaign will be the worked example for modders.

docs.title: Cockpits (HD and 3D)
docs.text:
A cockpit is an entry of the cockpits: section of a pack's rules; a ship uses it with cockpit: <id>. It can be 2D art, a 3D model, or both, and it says where the instruments go — as rectangles in a 2D design space, and for a 3D cockpit optionally as anchors on the model's surface, drawn in perspective.

cockpits:
  a:
    image: original:CockpitA.dll#12000   # 2D art: original, a pack image, or none
    design: [640, 480]                   # coordinate space of instruments (default 640, 480)
    model: models/cockpit.obj            # optional 3D cockpit around the pilot's eye
    model_offset: [0, 0, 0]              # metres from the eye (x right, y up, -z ahead)
    model_scale: 1
    instruments:
      message: [118, 12, 410, 24]
      radar_front: [111, 332, 60, 60]    # the round glass of the scope
      radar_rear: [473, 332, 60, 60]
      mfd: [246, 338, 156, 82]
      gauge1: [243, 299, 26, 26]         # speed
      gauge2: [288, 299, 26, 26]         # energy
      gauge3: [333, 299, 26, 26]         # shields
      gauge4: [378, 299, 26, 26]         # hull
Key Default Meaning image — Asset reference of the 2D art, drawn over the whole design space; none for no 2D art. design [640, 480] The size of the coordinate space the instruments use. The art is stretched to it whatever its pixel size. model none Asset reference of a 3D cockpit model. model_offset [0, 0, 0] Where the model's origin sits relative to the pilot's eye, in metres. model_scale 1 Model units → metres. instruments — name: [x, y, w, h] in design space. Names: message, radar_front, radar_rear, mfd, gauge1–gauge4, power, systems, status (the throttle/speed line; without it the line is plain screen text at the top left). A rectangle more than five times wider than tall is a strip and gets the instrument's one-line form (below). anchors none 3D cockpits: name: {at, normal, size} — the instrument drawn in perspective on the model (below).

All instrument text — MFD pages, the message line, gauge labels, the power and systems labels — is sized to fit its instrument's box, so a small rectangle gets small text rather than text spilling out of it.

docs.title: Shield rings
docs.text: Each radar scope carries a ring just inside its edge showing a shield facing: the front scope the fore shield, the rear scope the aft. Green above 66 %, amber above 33 %, red below, blinking red when the facing is down. Size the radar_front / radar_rear rectangles to the scope glass and the ring sits on its rim.

docs.title: The power and systems instruments (Stage 2)
docs.text:
Instrument Shows power Four columns: B-<level> and S-<level> (beam and shield charge setting, A–E, one cell lit per level), then F and A bars for the fore and aft shields as a fraction of their balanced capacity (red below 25 %; the favoured facing's label is white). When the power budget is fully used, used/budget appears in yellow. status The throttle, speed and drive/system flags line (THR 20% -274 m/s VCT BURN …), fitted to the rectangle and clipped with .. when long. strips In a strip, power reads B-<level> S-<level> F<fore %> A<aft %> (red when a facing is below 25 %), and systems lists only the systems that are not plain OK in their lamp colours, or SYSTEMS OK. The interceptor cockpits put status, power and systems in the two strips of the top display bar. systems One lamp per fitted system with a three-letter label (ENG, MAN, SEN, SHD, HYP, VCT, TRC, CLK, ECM, DCC): green working, bright cyan switched on, amber damaged, red knocked out (blinking while being repaired), dark destroyed.

A cockpit that does not place them still gets them: small panels at the top right of the cockpit's own design space (from 87.5 % of the design width, 9 % of its height down), with a dark backdrop over cockpit art. The original cockpits and the interceptor pack do not place them, so they appear there; the default campaign's 3D cockpit has bezels for both.

Radar rectangles enclose the scope's glass. Contacts are placed in the circle inscribed in the rectangle, so draw it tight around the round glass (centre on the painted crosshair). Over cockpit art the engine draws only the contacts — the art supplies the scope rings; on the glass HUD (no art) the engine adds two rings and an F/R label. The interceptor pack's values were measured from the original art to ±1 px.

A cockpit needs an image, a model, or both. Without a cockpit (or in the non-cockpit views) the HUD uses glass instruments in a default layout.

docs.title: How the screen is fitted
docs.text:
The design space is scaled as large as fits the window and centred (Layout::new(screen, design)): a 640×480 cockpit fills the height of a 16:9 window with space visible either side; a 1920×1080 design fills it exactly. So:

  • An HD repaint at the same proportions (2560×1920 for 640×480) needs no rule changes at all: just override the image.
  • A widescreen redesign sets design: [1920, 1080] and new instruments rectangles.

docs.title: A 3D cockpit instead of the overlay
docs.text:
With model, the cockpit is a 3D model drawn around the pilot's eye in the cockpit view (F1). It is drawn after the world with a fresh depth buffer, so the world never pokes through it, and with a 5 cm near plane, so struts right in front of the eye are not clipped. Model it in metres around the eye at the origin, +Y up, looking along −Z.

Its instruments can be placed two ways:

2D rectangle (instruments) Anchor (anchors) Drawn flat, over the view, at its design-space position into a texture, then mapped onto a rectangle on the model's surface, in perspective Window shape depends on the field of view matching the design (below) sits in its bezel at any window shape and field of view Used for 2D cockpits; any instrument without an anchor 3D cockpits with screens or bezels on the dashboard

An anchor is {at: [x, y, z], normal: [x, y, z], size: [w, h]} in metres from the eye: the centre of the instrument on the model, the surface's outward normal, and the instrument's width and height on the surface. Its "up" is world up projected onto the surface. An instrument with an anchor is drawn only on the surface in the cockpit view; its 2D rectangle still serves the other views and the fallback.

Field of view. The 3D view normally has a 60° vertical field. On a window narrower than the cockpit's design proportions (a 4:3 window with a 16:9 cockpit), that would cut off the cockpit's sides and misplace 2D instruments relative to their bezels, so the field widens until the design's full width fits (app::flight::cockpit_fov). Windows as wide as the design or wider keep 60°. Measure 2D rectangles for the camera they will be seen with: eye at the origin, looking −Z, 60° vertical field, at the design aspect. Anchored instruments do not need this.

The default campaign's Guard rockets fly from one, an art-deco dashboard (original-free, generated by tools/default_assets/models.py). The generator writes both placements, measured from the bezels it builds, to models/guard_cockpit.instruments.yaml, from which they are copied into the rules:

cockpits:
  guard:
    image: none
    model: models/guard_cockpit.obj
    model_offset: [0, 0, 0]
    design: [1280, 720]
    instruments:
      message: [404, 474, 472, 26]
      radar_front: [101, 540, 155, 156]
      mfd: [548, 514, 184, 186]
      power: [292, 628, 196, 64]
      systems: [792, 632, 196, 32]
      # … radar_rear, gauge1–gauge4
    anchors:
      message: {at: [0, -0.1729, -0.8497], normal: [0, 0.342, 0.9397], size: [0.6449, 0.0351]}
      mfd: {at: [0, -0.311, -0.7995], normal: [0, 0.342, 0.9397], size: [0.2445, 0.2218]}
      # … one per instrument
ships:
  comet:
    cockpit: guard

To give an original ship a 3D cockpit, a mod adds only:

cockpits:
  a:
    image: none                    # or keep the art and add the model on top
    model: models/lightning_pit.obj
    design: [1280, 720]
    # … new instruments in 1280×720, and anchors (or place them with F12, below)

docs.title: The cockpit layout editor (F12)
docs.text:
In the cockpit view of any ship with a cockpit, F12 opens the layout editor; the battle pauses while it is open.

Key / mouse Effect Tab / Shift+Tab Select the next / previous instrument (its name is shown at the top). 2D instrument: drag inside Move it. 2D instrument: drag the corner Resize it. 2D instrument: arrow keys Nudge 1 design pixel (Shift: 10). 3D (anchored) instrument: click the dashboard Place it there: a ray from the eye through the cursor is intersected with the cockpit model; the hit point becomes the anchor's centre and the hit face's normal its facing. Mouse wheel, + / - Grow / shrink the selected instrument by 5 % (2D about its centre; 3D keeps its proportions). S Save. F12 or Esc Leave the editor (unsaved changes stay for this flight only).

Save writes a small addon into the user's mods folder, <user data>/mods/<campaign>-cockpit-<cockpit id>/, with a pack.yaml (kind: addon, targets: [<campaign>]) and rules/cockpit-layout.yaml holding the cockpit's instruments and anchors. It loads with that campaign from then on and overrides the original layout key by key; delete the folder (or disable the pack) to go back. To ship a layout with your own mod, copy cockpit-layout.yaml into its rules/.

Status: the 3D cockpit path, anchors and the editor are implemented; the on-screen checks are manual tests MT-2-14 to MT-2-17.

Open a model straight in the viewer: openinterceptor --model <ship id or mesh name>. In the viewer, W cycles solid / solid + wireframe / wireframe, [ ] select faces (Shift: ten at a time) and show each face's number, corner count, texture, flags, overlay layer and UVs, I labels every face towards the camera, and O hides overlay-flagged faces.

docs.title: Make your first mod
docs.text: A walkthrough that builds a new, original-free campaign from the default campaign (Perils of the Void). No programming and no X-COM data needed.

docs.title: 1. Copy the default campaign
docs.text:
MODS="$HOME/Library/Application Support/OpenInterceptor/mods"   # Linux: ~/.local/share/openinterceptor/mods
mkdir -p "$MODS"
cp -R packs/default "$MODS/frontier"

docs.title: 2. Give it its own id
docs.text:
Edit frontier/pack.yaml:

# yaml-language-server: $schema=../schemas/pack.schema.json
id: frontier
name: Frontier
version: "0.1"
description: My first OpenInterceptor mod
kind: campaign
format: 2
requires_original: false

The copy is a campaign of its own: on the launcher, Tab switches between Perils of the Void and Frontier (or start with --campaign frontier). Only one campaign loads at a time, so the copy's ship ids do not clash with the original's. To change a few values of the default campaign instead of copying all of it, make a small addon (kind: addon, targets: [default]) that only contains the changed keys — see Packs.

Editor help. The first line of every file names its JSON Schema. The copied files point at the repository's schemas/ folder. In your mods folder, run openinterceptor --write-schemas "$MODS/schemas" once and change the first lines to ../schemas/pack.schema.json (in pack.yaml) and ../../schemas/rules.schema.json or ../../schemas/scenario.schema.json (in rules/ and scenarios/): your editor then offers completion, hover help and live checking.

docs.title: 3. Change a ship
docs.text:
In frontier/rules/ships.yaml, make the Comet faster, give it a third gun and fit a tractor ray:

ships:
  comet:
    name: Comet Mk II
    max_speed: 700
    beams: [blaster, blaster, heat_ray]
    systems+: [tractor]       # adds to the Comet's list (which already has ecm)

Only the keys you change need to appear if you edit the copy in place; a typo such as max_sped is reported with its file and line, with a suggestion. Power, systems and damage rules are in rules/systems.yaml — see Rulesets.

docs.title: 4. Make the enemy smarter (optional)
docs.text:
The saucers fly the behaviours in rules/behaviours.yaml. Make the scouts aim better and run away when badly hurt, at every difficulty level:

behaviours:
  saucer_scout:
    skill: {aim: 0.6, reaction: 0.6s}
    transitions:
      - {from: engage, to: dodge, when: "hit_recently(0.3s) and random(0.35)"}
      - {from: dodge, to: engage, when: "time_in_state > 2.5s"}
      - {from: "*", to: flee, when: "hull < 30%"}

See Behaviours and conditions.

docs.title: 5. Add a scenario
docs.text:
Create frontier/scenarios/patrol.yaml (see Scenarios):

# yaml-language-server: $schema=../../schemas/scenario.schema.json
id: frontier-patrol
title: Frontier patrol
player: comet
order: 5
objects:
  station:
    class: guard_station
    position: [0, 0, -1500]
  r1:
    class: scout_saucer
    ai: enemy
    position: [0, 300, -5000]
    speed: 250

docs.title: 6. Bring your own model (optional)
docs.text: Export an OBJ + MTL from Blender (Forward −Z, Up Y, metres) into frontier/models/, then point a ship at it: model: models/hornet.obj. The default campaign's own models are generated by the Python scripts in tools/default_assets/, which are a worked example of building models in code. Textures referenced by map_Kd are relative to the .mtl file. See Models and textures.

docs.title: 7. Validate and play
docs.text:
openinterceptor --check --no-original                       # checks every campaign; fix anything it reports
openinterceptor --no-original --campaign frontier           # "Frontier patrol" is on the launcher

Use the Model viewer to inspect your models, then fly the scenario. D on the launcher changes the difficulty level (cadet … space ace).

docs.title: Looks: model sets, debris and effects
docs.text:
How an object looks in every state is kept apart from what it is. A ship or object class names a model set (model_set: comet); the model set names its model, the texture swaps for its damage levels and named states, the debris set it breaks into and the effect of its explosion. Several classes can share a look, and a remaster can replace a look without touching any class. Keys from src/content/looks.rs; every field with type and default: Mod file reference.

modelsets:
  comet:
    intact: models/comet.obj
    damage:                                   # texture swaps as the hull falls
      - {below: 66%, textures: {guard_hull: textures/guard_hull_scorched.png}}
      - {below: 33%, textures: {guard_hull: textures/guard_hull_burnt.png}}
    debris: comet                             # the debris set used when it explodes
    destroyed_effect: explosion_small
debris:
  comet:
    pieces: [models/comet_debris1.obj, models/comet_debris2.obj, models/comet_debris3.obj]
    pick: [2, 3]                              # how many pieces, chosen at random
    speed: [20, 60]                           # m/s, thrown outwards
    spin: [30, 120]                           # degrees per second
    life: 20s
    chunks: {models: [models/chunk1.obj], count: 6, speed: [40, 120]}
effects:
  explosion_small: {size: 2.5, duration: 1.2s, color: [1, 0.6, 0.2], shockwave: false}
ships:
  comet:
    model_set: comet

The Stage 1 keys still work: a class with model: (and debris: as a list of pieces) and no model_set gets a simple model set of its own.

docs.title: Model sets
Debris sets
docs.text:
Key Meaning pieces Piece models, in the object's own model space: placed at the object, they reassemble it. Each piece starts where it belongs and flies off with the object's velocity plus a random outward push. pick [min, max] pieces thrown, chosen at random without repeats (default: all of them). speed, spin [min, max] outward speed (m/s, default 20–60) and tumble (°/s, default 30–120). life How long the pieces last (default 15 s); wreckage darkens as it cools over its last third. chunks Generic rubble: {models: […], count, speed: [min, max]} scattered from the centre (default none).

The default campaign's generator (tools/default_assets/models.py) cuts each model into its pieces with planes, so they fit together exactly; the scorched, burnt and wrecked textures come from textures.py.

docs.title: Effects
docs.text:
Key Meaning size Fireball size: a multiple of the object's radius (for a missile's explosion, metres). duration How long it lasts. color Fireball colour. shockwave true adds an expanding ring of light in the wreck's plane. sound A sound event name (from sounds:) or asset, played with the effect.

Effects are used by model sets (destroyed_effect; without one, the effect named explosion — a pack may define it, otherwise the engine's: size 2.5, 1.6 s, orange) and by missiles (explosion, sized in metres; without one, a 25 m, 0.8 s fireball).

docs.title: The interceptor pack's looks
docs.text: packs/interceptor/rules/looks.yaml restates the original's wreck table: 28 named wreck sets of up to five chunk meshes each (sets with fewer chunks repeat the first), plus generic rubble, the alien body parts that float in alien wrecks, and the shock-wave meshes. The file holds only names and numbers — set names and original: mesh references read from Interceptor.exe (verified) — never the meshes; which class uses which set follows the names (derived). The original's explosions are XSPT sprite animations, not yet decoded, so the fireballs are the engine's (DEV-034).

docs.title: Checking looks
docs.text:
• Model viewer: D cycles a class's looks — intact, each damage level, each state, and the debris pieces pulled apart from the centre — with the look's name on the info line.
  • --check loads every swapped texture and every debris piece and chunk.
  • The debris-showcase scenario (both campaigns) lines up every class at 2 % hull: the damage textures show at once, and one shot each shows the explosion, shock wave and debris.

docs.title: Missions
docs.text:
A scenario places fixed objects. A mission describes a battle by roles — groups of craft whose classes, counts and arrivals vary — and says when it is won, lost or drawn, and what happens then. Implemented in Stage 3 (part 1, app 0.3.0): src/content/mission.rs (the definitions), src/mission/ (the runtime, architecture), src/script/battle.rs (the battle conditions) and src/script/action.rs (outcome actions).

Missions are a rules section, missions:, so they live in any rules folder (by convention missions/*.yaml) and get everything rules offer: inherit, variants per difficulty level and {per_level: […]} values. They appear on the launcher as Mission: … entries and start with --mission <id>; the strategy layer (Stage 4) will generate them from the campaign.

docs.title: A worked example
docs.text:
# missions/missions.yaml
missions:
