docs.text: damage: How the warhead's damage lands normal (default) On the shield facing that was hit, then armour, then hull. bypass_shields Ignores shields: straight to armour and hull (the original's Permeator). enveloping Spread over both shield facings, as if the whole surface were hit.

docs.title: Point defence
docs.text:
A ship or object with point_defence carries automatic guns that shoot at the nearest hostile missile in range — decoys included, since the guns cannot tell them apart:

objects:
  guard_station:
    point_defence: {range: 1.2km, rate: 4, chance: 40%, energy: 3}
Key Default Meaning range 800 m Reach. rate 3 Shots per second. chance 35 % Chance a shot destroys the missile, rolled on the world's seeded generator (battles replay identically). energy 4 Energy per shot, from the ship's capacitor; no energy, no shot.

Each shot draws a tracer and plays the point_defence event sound. Point defence is fitted to the Patton, the X-COM freighter and the bases (interceptor), and to the dreadnought and the stations (default); the numbers are derived (DEV-038).

docs.title: Mines
docs.text: An object with kind: mine and a behaviour whose state does do: mine waits until a hostile is within the state's range, then detonates its first missile rack as the warhead: an area blast reaching four times the warhead's proximity_radius (at least 100 m), dealing its proximity_damage falling off linearly with distance, enveloping — and the mine is gone. See Stations and modules › Mines for a complete example.

docs.title: In the two campaigns
docs.text: Campaign Missiles interceptor X-Winder (homing), Sidestep, Permeator (bypass_shields), Fusion, Enveloping torpedo, Parallax torpedo (2 decoys), Passive Cloaking torpedo (cloaked_wait), Doppelganger — the special behaviours follow the original's descriptions (derived); the Super Avenger's testbed load carries one of each. default Seeker rockets, atomic torpedoes, cluster rockets (Thunderbolt), decoy rockets (Meteor), Dominion space-mine warheads (dominion-raid).

docs.title: The original game
docs.text:
X-COM: Interceptor (MicroProse, May 1998) combines a real-time strategy layer, where the player runs X-COM's bases on a frontier of star systems, with a 3D space-combat simulator, where the player flies one ship with AI wingmen.

This section records what the engine has to reproduce and how the data on the CD is stored. Facts carry a source and, where they were worked out rather than read, a confidence:

Mark Meaning verified Checked against the data (parsed, rendered, or counted) derived Reasoned from strings, field names or values; not yet proven in play unknown Not yet determined

Sources: the release Readme.txt, the INI files and the string tables on the CD (read as data, never reproduced here), the 1998 demo readme, a published walkthrough, Wikipedia and MobyGames. UFOpaedia's Interceptor pages were not reachable by automated tools and remain to be checked.

  • Gameplay: ships, stations, weapons, missions, strategy layer.
  • Controls: the original key, mouse and joystick layout.
  • CD layout: what every file holds.
  • Formats: how each file type is read.

docs.title: CD layout
docs.text:
What is on the CD and what the engine reads. Paths are relative to the Game/ folder of a CD copy. Sizes are approximate.

Path Holds Read by the engine Resources/xobjects1.dll, xobjects2.dll All 3D models (XMSH), their textures (XTXR) and effect sprites (XSPT), as Win32 resources Yes (Stage 1) Resources/CockpitA.dll, CockpitB.dll, CockpitC.dll Cockpit art per hull (TARG = TGA): the 640×480 frame and instrument parts Yes (Stage 1) Resources/CockpitMisc.dll Shared cockpit/HUD parts (TARG) Yes (Stage 1–2) Resources/SpritesDLL.dll ~1,700 small TGA sprites: icons, HUD elements Stage 2–5 Resources/WrappersDLL.dll Full-screen menu and strategy screens (TARG) Stage 5 ProgramFiles/Interceptor.exe The original program. Read only for its string tables (object names) Strings only ProgramFiles/xcgen.dll The original 3D engine ("XCGEN") Never run ProgramFiles/GameSettings.ini Balance data: weapons, equipment, hulls, tech tree, modules, stations, scores Yes (Stage 1) ProgramFiles/Think.ini Alien strategic AI Stage 4 ProgramFiles/soundfx.ini Sound-effect table Stage 2 ProgramFiles/MPSettings.INI, NetSettings.ini Multiplayer arenas and network settings Deferred ProgramFiles/3DObjects/*.tga Lens flares, reticles, sun and star sprites Yes (Stage 1) ProgramFiles/Animations/mfdanim.mps MFD animation (format unknown) Stage 2+ ProgramFiles/SoundFX/{SpaceFlight,Chatter,Gadgets,Wrappers}/ Sound effects and radio chatter, MS-ADPCM WAV Stage 1–3 ProgramFiles/Loops/*.wav Music loops (cruise, battle, …) as PCM WAV Stage 5 ProgramFiles/Text/*.txt UI strings, encyclopedia, names, news, credits Stage 3–5 Animations/*.smk Cut-scenes, Smacker video Stage 5 ../CD Audio/*.aiff Red Book music tracks, extracted by the player as AIFF-C Stage 5 SETUP.EXE, *.cab, DirectX/, IE4_0Setup/, EReg/ Installer, DirectX 5, Internet Explorer 4, registration Never

The CD's ProgramFiles/ folder is already an installed layout, so the engine reads the CD copy directly; no installer step is needed.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text: Two tables: what the original game used (sources: the 1998 demo readme for keys, the release Readme.txt for mouse and joystick, the game's bindable-action list), and what OpenInterceptor binds by default (from the single ACTIONS table in src/input/mod.rs, which also drives the controls menu, so the tables below cannot drift from the game). Every engine binding can be changed in the in-game Controls menu or in bindings.yaml.

docs.title: Original keyboard defaults
docs.text:
Action Key Nose down / up Up / Down arrow Turn (yaw) left / right Left / Right arrow Roll left / right NumPad 7 / NumPad 9 Throttle up / down 10 % + / - Full throttle / zero throttle Backspace / \ Reverse throttle toggle Z Afterburner (hold) Tab Hyperspace out H Next / previous target T / Y Closest enemy / target in sights R / G Fire beams / fire missile Enter / Space Beam link mode (link / full / unlink) X Next / previous / default MFD mode > / < / Esc Beam / shield charge rate F9 / F10 Shield balance S Power to shields / to weapons ; / ' Wingman menu, repeat last message ], L Wingmen: fire at will / attack my target / ignore / evasive / retreat Shift+F / A / I / E / R Views: cockpit, full forward, left, right, rear-left, rear-right F1 – F6 Chase camera auto / manual F7 / F8 Chase camera move Ins/Del, PgUp/PgDn, Home/End (zoom), NumPad 5 (reset) Pause / quit P / Alt+Q

The original also had bindable actions with no documented default: slide left/right/up/down (VCT), tractor, cloak, ECM, match speed, cycle beam, cycle missile, letterbox, include base modules.

Mouse (release readme, not remappable in the original): "Nose Down = Mouse Back, Nose Up = Mouse Up", left/right = turn, left button = beams, right button = missiles.

Joystick and rudder: stick left/right yaws and the rudder rolls; Alt+J swaps to an aircraft layout. The hat switch drives the VCT.

docs.title: OpenInterceptor defaults
docs.text: Key and button names are those used in bindings.yaml (case does not matter). Shift+F is a keyboard chord; LeftShoulder+A is a gamepad chord (hold the left shoulder, press A). Since Stage 2 every action of the original has a default except letterbox, include base modules and quit (Alt+Q), which are still unbound (they arrive with the views and the strategy layer; the pause menu quits).

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
Action (bindings.yaml name) Label Default keys Default gamepad Notes mfd_next Next MFD page Period DpadRight the > key; pages Target, Weapons, Status, Systems, Nav mfd_prev Previous MFD page Comma DpadLeft the < key next_nav Next nav point N — engine extension (DEV-002) pause Pause P Start menu Menu Escape LeftShoulder+Start pause menu: Esc resume, R restart, K controls, L back to launcher mouse_flight Mouse flight on/off C — toggles mouse flight (hides and confines the cursor)

Shift chords and held keys. A Shift+ chord only fires with Shift held, and a plain key only fires without it, so F and Shift+F can do different things. While Shift is held, a key that belongs to some Shift chord is ignored by the held actions bound to it: Shift+E orders the wingmen to evade without also rolling the ship on E.

Mouse flight (after C): cursor offset from the screen centre steers — moving the cursor down lowers the nose (the readme's "Nose Down = Mouse Back"), right turns right. Left button fires beams, right button fires a missile. mouse_range (pixels for full deflection, default 200) and mouse_invert (true = moving up lowers the nose) are in bindings.yaml and the controls menu.

docs.title: OpenInterceptor gamepad defaults
docs.text:
XInput layout on every platform (Platform layer). The pad has two layers: the buttons on their own, and the same buttons while the left shoulder (LB) is held. A button used as a modifier in any chord does nothing on its own while held — that is why previous target, alone among the Stage 1 pad bindings, moved to LB + RB (DEV-028).

Control On its own With LB held Left stick Yaw (X) and pitch (Y; forward = nose down) — or roll and pitch in the aircraft layout Right stick Roll (X) and vertical VCT slide (Y) — or yaw and slide in the aircraft layout Right trigger / left trigger Fire beams (hold) / fire missile Right shoulder (RB) Next target Previous target A Afterburner (hold) Hyperspace out / abort B Brake (hold) Shield balance X Match speed Tractor beam Y Chase view Cloaking device D-pad up / down Throttle up / down 10 % Power to beams / power to shields D-pad left / right Previous / next MFD page Beam charge / shield charge rate Back Beam link mode ECM Start Pause Menu Left stick click Next missile type Wingman menu Right stick click Nearest enemy Target in sights

Wingman orders other than the menu have no default pad chord: open the menu with LB + left stick click, then choose with the d-pad and A (B closes it). Stick options (in the controls menu or options: in bindings.yaml): stick_layout: space (default, as the original joystick) or aircraft (the original's Alt+J swap: left stick rolls, right stick yaws), invert_pitch, dead_zone.

In the launcher: D-pad chooses, A or Start starts, Y switches campaign, Back quits.

docs.title: The controls menu
docs.text:
Reached from the launcher (Controls (keyboard, gamepad, mouse)) and from the in-flight pause menu (Esc, then K). The model is input::editor::Editor; the screen is app::controls (Input architecture).

  • Rows are the actions, grouped as in the tables above, followed by the device settings: stick dead zone, pull back to dive, stick layout, mouse flight range and mouse invert.
  • Each action has four cells: Key, Alt key, Gamepad, Alt gamepad.
  • Enter (pad A) on a key cell waits for a key — Shift may be held for a chord; on a pad cell it waits for a button, or for a modifier held and a second button pressed (a chord). Esc cancels; a capture gives up after 8 seconds. On a setting, Enter (or Left/Right) changes it.
  • Delete or Backspace (pad X) clears the cell; D (pad Y) restores the action's defaults; Shift+D restores every default.
  • Binding a key or chord that another action used takes it away from that action; the status line names the action that lost it.
  • Up/Down (d-pad) select, Left/Right or Tab move between cells, PageUp/PageDown (LB/RB) page. Esc (pad B) leaves: the bindings apply at once and are saved to bindings.yaml.

docs.title: bindings.yaml
docs.text:
Created with every default on first run in the user data folder — macOS ~/Library/Application Support/OpenInterceptor/bindings.yaml, Linux $XDG_DATA_HOME/openinterceptor/bindings.yaml (default ~/.local/share/openinterceptor/), and rewritten in full whenever the controls menu saves. Anything not mentioned keeps its default. A bindings.ini from an earlier build is read once, and its bindings are saved as bindings.yaml.

keyboard:
  fire_beams: [Enter, LeftControl]    # a list: several keys per action
  tractor: [Shift+T]                  # Shift+ makes a chord
  ecm: []                             # an empty list unbinds the action
gamepad:
  hyperspace: [LeftShoulder+A]        # Modifier+Button chord
  fire_beams: [RightTrigger]
options:
  dead_zone: 0.15
  invert_pitch: false
  stick_layout: space                 # space | aircraft
  mouse_range: 200
  mouse_invert: false

Run with OI_DEBUG_KEYS=1 to print the name of each key you press.

docs.title: The space simulator
docs.text: Each battle is one 3D arena. The player flies one ship; the other X-COM ships are AI wingmen. There are no in-mission navigation points: travel between systems happens on the strategy map, and the player leaves a battle by hyperspace (H, with an abortable countdown). (derived from the bindable action list and the walkthrough)

docs.title: Damage model
docs.text:
Three layers: shields (fore and aft facings), then armour, then hull. The cockpit reports per-system damage and repair (shield generator, manoeuvring, sensors, engines, hyperdrive, tractor, cloak, VCT, damage control, ECM). (derived from cockpit strings)

In OpenInterceptor (Stage 2, implemented): every fitted system has hit points; damage past the armour also strikes one system at random; systems work at full, half or no effect, can be destroyed for the battle, and are repaired worst first (faster with a damage control computer). Engines and manoeuvring both out leaves a ship disabled. The thresholds are engine values (DEV-029). Rules: Rulesets › systems; behaviour: Simulation › systems.

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
One power supply feeds beam weapons and shields. Each has a recharge setting with five steps (A–E) cycled with F9 / F10; ; and ' move power between them; S cycles shield balance (equal / full forward / full aft). Tractor, cloak and ECM also draw power; beams cannot fire while the tractor is on. (GameSettings.ini BeamRechargeRate, ShieldRechargeRate; strings)

In OpenInterceptor (Stage 2, implemented): all of the above, with the original's keys (Controls). The charge tables are the original's (verified); how many steps may be high at once — the power budget — and the start levels are engine values (DEV-024). The tractor beam tows a target and a disabled ship held at the moment of a hyperjump is captured; the cloak hides the ship from enemy sensors beyond its range and is dropped by firing (DEV-025); ECM and the cloak make homing missiles lose their target; the hyperdrive counts down and can be aborted (DEV-026). Wingmen obey all five orders of the comms menu plus a status report.

docs.title: Flight model
docs.text:
Per hull, GameSettings.ini gives roll, yaw and pitch rates, an angular damping value ("0 tight – 10 loose"), a LockSpeed ("speed at which pitch and yaw rates are zero") and a MaxSpeed. Turn rate therefore falls as speed rises: the central handling idea. Speeds are in metres per second (weapon speeds are commented in m/s). The afterburner has Boost and Cost values whose units are not yet confirmed (derived: +150 m/s for 50 energy per second).

VCT (Vector Control Thrusters) is fitted equipment that lets a ship slide sideways and vertically. Alien ships have it, which is why they out-turn missiles.

docs.title: Missile lock
docs.text: Three sensor settings give a lock time and a lock cone: A 2.5 s, B 2.0 s, C 1.5 s, with widening cones. They correspond (derived) to the three targeting systems: Standard, Emissions and AATS. Some missiles need a minimum targeting system.

docs.title: Player hulls
docs.text: Hull Section Mounts (beam / missile / special) Character X-1A Lightning II Ship_IntType1 2 / 2 / 2 Fastest turning, fragile S-2 Firestar Ship_IntType2 4 / 3 / 4 Middle weight M-3 Super Avenger Ship_IntType3 4 / 5 / 6 Heavy; only hull for the Nova Bomb

docs.title: Alien ships
docs.text: Ship Role Wraith Light saucer fighter Spectre Multirole saucer Phantasm Heavy beam saucer; leads assaults Shade Elite non-saucer fighter: accumulator shields, VCT, cloak, ECM Harbinger Tug; tows cargo, tries to capture disabled ships Spirit Freighter; launches drones Drone Unmanned, fast, unarmoured Probes Sensor, intel jammer, comm jammer Mines Explosive, beam, missile

docs.title: Others
docs.text: Pirates (the Kabron) and corporations fly the same three human hulls in their own colours, plus freighters. The Patton-class research cruiser is an unarmed former warship.

docs.title: Stations
docs.text: X-COM bases are modular (hub plus hangar, personnel, medical, training, cargo, communications, downlinks, sensors, shield generators, ECM, tractor, probe launch, damage control, and beam/missile defence modules). Also: corporate outposts, Ore Processing Plants (OPPs), alien bases (a hub with pods; destroy the hub to destroy the base), alien outposts and mining platforms, pirate bases, the arms dealer, the science station, the Nova science station, the alien Doomsday weapon and the portal.

docs.title: Weapons
docs.text:
Beams: Laser Cannon, Heavy Laser, Gatling Laser, Tracer Cannon (continuous), Tracking Tracer, Phase Cannon (anti-shield), and alien Plasma Cannon, Tachyon Pulser (shields and engines only, for capture) and Psi Blaster. Beams can be linked, fired fully, or unlinked (X).

Missiles: X-winder (basic heat seeker), Elerium Torpedo, Permeator (bypasses shields), Sidestep (own thrusters), Enveloping Fusion Torpedo (damage spread over the surface), Parallax Torpedo (two decoys), Passive Cloaking Torpedo (dropped; waits cloaked), Doppelganger (a decoy copy of your ship), Fusion Missile (anti-station) and the Nova Bomb.

Defensive equipment: ECM pods, cloaking device, tractor beam (0.25 km), damage control computer.

docs.title: Missions
docs.text: Defend outpost / OPP / base, defend freighter convoys, defend probe or fleet, attack alien fleet, attack freighter or tug convoys, attack alien OPP / outpost / base / probe, attack the portal fleet, patrol, and the two-part final mission. Side missions: rogue freighter, pirate raiders, defend a pirate base, the hijacked Nova Bomb prototype, the arms dealer, survey a system. After a battle: debrief and score (MissionScores). Disabled ships can be tractored home for salvage.

docs.title: Strategy layer
docs.text: A star map of the Frontier with time compression; bases and modules; research done on Earth and sent via downlinks; manufacturing and purchase; pilots; probes; money from corporate protection payments and salvage; an alien strategic AI with its own budget split between research, goods and the Doomsday project (Think.ini). The tech tree is the R_* sections of GameSettings.ini.

docs.title: Multiplayer
docs.text: Dogfight arenas (deep space, asteroids, black hole, around each station type) and team modes (MPSettings.INI, NetSettings.ini). Deferred: see deviations.

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The specification states how OpenInterceptor behaves, precisely enough to build and test against. It has three parts:

  • Requirements, grouped by area, each implementing one or more features;
  • the mod formats and design pages, normative for the files a modder writes;
  • the original data formats, normative for reading the player's CD.

Specification version 1.0.0 (168 requirements). Changes are listed in the change history.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Area Code Requirements Features Flight FLT 12 Flight Combat CMB 21 Combat Cockpit & HUD HUD 12 Cockpit & HUD Controls & control console CON 21 Controls & control console Missions MSN 12 Missions Strategy & logistics STR 27 Strategy & logistics Campaigns CPN 12 Campaigns Modding toolkit MOD 20 Modding toolkit Compatibility (original data) CMP 13 Compatibility (original data) Platforms PLT 6 Platforms Testbed & tools TST 12 Testbed & tools

Planned interfaces: Console protocol.

docs.title: Reading a requirement
docs.text:
Each requirement is a heading R-<AREA>-NNN Title with:

  • the behaviour in MUST / SHOULD / MAY terms and a one-line rationale;
  • Implements: the feature(s) it serves;
  • Status: implemented or planned;
  • Verified by: unit-test names (module::test_name) and manual test IDs (MT-…) where implemented;
  • Reverse-engineered: yes when it was written from the existing code rather than ahead of it;
  • See: the normative format page or architecture page;
  • an Open box where the material is thin and a decision is still needed.

Requirement IDs are permanent. In the Rapid Prototyping workflow the specification moves before the code: a request becomes a feature, then requirements, then issues.

docs.title: Revision history
docs.text: Version Date Change 1.0.0 2026-11-11 Bootstrap: requirement pages for eleven areas (168 requirements), the planned console protocol; format pages adopted as normative

docs.title: Console protocol
docs.text:
Status: planned. The messages the game and a control console exchange. The console is the tablet page served by the game (F-CON-004); later, a physical panel over USB serial (F-CON-007). Requirements: R-CON-009 – R-CON-021.

The message names, their direction and their rates below are decided. Field lists are a first draft, marked planned: implementation (interlude items C1–C4) fixes them, and this page is updated in the same change.

docs.title: Transport
docs.text:
• Each message is one JSON object with a type field.
  • WebSocket (first transport): the game serves the console page and the socket over HTTP on the local network only, port 8765 by default and changeable in the settings. The console is off by default (decision D2).
  • USB serial (later, for an Arduino panel): the same messages, one per line. The protocol never depends on the transport.

docs.title: Session
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Console
    participant G as Game
    C->>G: hello (pairing code)
    G->>C: welcome
    G->>C: catalogue
    G->>C: theme
    loop while paired
        G-->>C: telemetry (20 Hz)
        G-->>C: contacts (5 Hz)
        G-->>C: model (once per target class)
        G-->>C: event (as it happens)
        C->>G: action {name, value}
    end

docs.title: Messages
docs.text:
Message Direction When Carries (planned fields) hello console → game On connect The pairing code shown by the game; a client name and protocol version. welcome game → console Code accepted Protocol version, the active campaign. A wrong code closes the connection. catalogue game → console After welcome; again whenever the craft changes The action catalogue (R-CON-007): each action's id, name, group, description and value kind, and its availability for the current craft (a feature the craft lacks, such as cloak or ECM not fitted or no missiles, is marked not fitted). Every function group is always listed (R-CON-019). theme game → console After welcome; again when the campaign or craft changes The active pack's console theme (R-CON-020): colours, fonts, frames and images taken from the pack's own console assets — never original art (R-CON-021). telemetry game → console 20 Hz The player craft's state: speed with drift components, throttle, energy, shields fore and aft, hull, power settings, system conditions, weapons and missiles, lock, current target. contacts game → console 5 Hz Radar contacts with position relative to the player, faction and kind; nav points. model game → console Once per target class, when first targeted The target's mesh, decimated, for the viewport (R-CON-015). The orientation itself travels in telemetry. action console → game On a tap or slider move {name, value}: a catalogue action and its value (a press, or a level for sliders). Unknown or unavailable actions are ignored (R-CON-011). event game → console As it happens Messages and events (system damaged, missile lock, shield down, mission result). 
{"type": "action", "name": "power_shields_up", "value": 1}

The action name in the example is illustrative; names come from the catalogue.

docs.title: Open
docs.text:
• Field names and units of every message; the protocol version scheme.
  • The pairing code's length and lifetime, and how the game shows it.
  • The decimation budget for model, and whether textures are sent.
  • Line framing and the message subset for the serial transport.
  • The theme's file format in a pack.

docs.title: Coverage matrix
docs.text:
Status: design check, 2026-11-10. For every system of the original (analysis): the construct that expresses it, where the interceptor mod gets the data, and the simplified equivalent in the default campaign. The second table goes the other way: features the default campaign adds, and what they mean for interceptor. A row with no construct would be a gap in the format. There are none; the open items at the end are data the original hides in code, which must be recovered, not format features that are missing.

Data source key: INI = imported from the original INI files by inherit: original:… (mod files themselves are YAML); TXT = original text by reference; AUTH = authored in the mod from the strategy guide and play-testing (the original hard-codes it); EXE = a table read from the executable during analysis and written into the mod as data.

docs.title: Open items (data the original keeps in code)
docs.text:
These need the strategy guide, careful play of the original, or both; each becomes a work item in Stage 5 with its source recorded (verified/derived) in the mod's comments:

  1. The meaning of each MissionScores index (values are data, indices are code).
  2. Exact squadron compositions per mission type, tech level and difficulty (the guide's tables are partly illegible).
  3. Star count, planet size and sensor-radius tables for map generation.
  4. Salary, recruitment and psionics-by-rank modifiers.
  5. The alien tech-level cost mapping and the Doomsday cost/time columns.
  6. Station hit-point chart meaning (HP1..HP4, SD).
  7. The three-ring effect meshes (1ASH* etc.): shield flash or jump effect.
  8. Whether overlay-face low bits on station hubs are state groups.

Each is a data question with a reasonable fallback (the guide's legible values, or a documented estimate marked derived), so none blocks the format or the stages.

docs.title: Format: behaviours and scripting
docs.text: Status: Tier 1 behaviours and conditions (object context) implemented in Stage 2; actions, the battle and campaign contexts, the remaining manoeuvres, targeting preferences and Tier 2 are design. Replaces the open question on Scripting with a two-tier design; the Tier 2 language decision is taken at the start of Stage 3. The implemented form is documented for modders on Behaviours and conditions.

docs.title: Two tiers
docs.text:
Tier What Who needs it 1. Declarative Behaviours, missions and events written as YAML definitions, with a small condition and action language for the parts that vary (hull < 0.3, research(plasma), spawn(wave_2)). Implemented in-crate: a lexer, parser, type checker and interpreter of a few hundred lines each — itself a teaching example. Everything. Both shipped campaigns (interceptor, default) are written entirely in Tier 1. 2. Scripts Optional script files for behaviour Tier 1 cannot express (a boss with bespoke phases, a puzzle mission, a procedural campaign generator). Called through named hooks from Tier 1. Mods that want it.

Why not scripts for everything: Tier 1 definitions can be validated before play (every reference and type checked by --check), saved trivially (they are data), run deterministically at the fixed 60 Hz tick, and edited by someone who does not program. The original game's behaviour is hard-coded C++ whose logic is a fixed set of states and parameters, so Tier 1 is a natural fit for it.

docs.title: Conditions
docs.text:
A condition is an expression that evaluates to true or false. The same language is used in every when, requires, visible_when and if key across the format. Implemented for the object context (reference, architecture).

hull < 0.3 and not system_damaged(engines)
research(plasma_beam) and day >= 30
relation(cartel) <= -20 or flag(cartel_betrayed)
count(ships, faction: alien, class: fighter, within: 5km) >= 3
difficulty >= veteran
  • Values: numbers (with units m, km, s, min, h, day, %, converted to base units), booleans, ids as query arguments (plasma_beam), and the difficulty levels as ordered constants. (Implemented: all but strings, which no context needs yet.)
  • Operators: + - * /, comparisons, and or not, parentheses.
  • Functions: a fixed, documented query API per context (below). Unknown names, wrong argument types and misspelt ids are load errors, not run-time surprises.
  • No assignment, no loops, no user functions: a condition cannot change the game and always terminates.
Context Queries available (examples) Object (behaviours) — implemented hull, shields, energy, speed, has_target, target_distance, target_hull, target_disabled, target_is_player, time_in_state, hit_recently(t), random(p), system_damaged(x), threats(d), allies(d), missiles, difficulty, disabled, towing, prize_near(d). Not yet: target_class, ammo(x). Battle (missions) count(...), alive(name), destroyed(name), disabled(name), captured(name), time, objective(x), player_hull, near(a, b, d) Campaign (events, strategy) day, date, money, research(x), researching(x), module(x), owns(system), relation(faction), flag(x), counter(x), missions_won(type), losses(class), resource(x), threat(system), difficulty

random(p) draws from the game's seeded generator, so a replay or reload gives the same result.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
An action changes the game. Action lists appear in events, mission outcomes and behaviour transitions; they run in order.

spawn(wave_2)
message(@msg.convoy_spotted, from: freighter_1)
set_flag(cartel_betrayed); add(relation(cartel), -30); add(money, 250000)
unlock(research: alien_navigation); start_mission(nova_theft, system: kepler)

The action vocabulary per context is fixed and documented in the reference (Stage 3 and 4 implement it). As with queries, everything is checked at load time.

docs.title: Behaviours: behaviours: {<id>: …}
docs.text:
A behaviour is a state machine for one object: states, each running a built-in manoeuvre with parameters, and transitions with conditions. Built-in manoeuvres cover what the original AI does; their parameters are the tuning.

The implemented form (Stage 2):

behaviours:
  wraith:
    start: engage
    states:                        # state: manoeuvre and its parameters
      engage:
        do: attack
        range: 1.6km
        fire_cone: 3
        burst: {per_level: [0.6s, 0.8s, 1s, 1.2s, 1.5s]}
        pause: {per_level: [2s, 1.6s, 1.2s, 0.9s, 0.6s]}
        missiles: {per_level: [0, 0, 14s, 11s, 8s]}
      jink: {do: evade, duration: 2s}
      flee: {do: retreat, jump: true}
    transitions:                   # tried in order; from "*" = any state
      - {from: engage, to: jink, when: "hit_recently(0.3s) and random(0.4)"}
      - {from: jink, to: engage, when: "time_in_state > 2s"}
      - {from: "*", to: flee, when: "hull < 15% and difficulty >= veteran"}
    skill:
      aim: {per_level: [0.2, 0.35, 0.5, 0.65, 0.8]}
      reaction: {per_level: [1.3s, 1s, 0.8s, 0.6s, 0.4s]}
    variants:                      # per difficulty level: only what differs
      beginner: {transitions: [{from: engage, to: jink, when: "random(0.2)"}]}

Still design: targeting preferences (target: {player: 3, wingman: 2, freighter: 1}), more manoeuvre parameters (evade_when_hit, jink, lead, retreat to a point), and wingman orders as transitions. The original design sketch, in today's syntax:

behaviours:
  wraith:
    start: engage
    states:
      engage: {do: attack, range: 1.5km, fire_cone: 8, burst: 2s, evade_when_hit: true}
      evade: {do: evade, duration: 3s, jink: 40}
      flee: {do: retreat, to: nearest_friendly_base}
    transitions:
      - {from: engage, to: evade, when: "hit_recently(1s) and random(0.4)"}
      - {from: evade, to: engage, when: "time_in_state > 3s"}
      - {from: "*", to: flee, when: "hull < 25% and difficulty >= veteran"}
    target: {player: 3, wingman: 2, freighter: 1}     # targeting preferences, scored
    skill: {aim: 0.6, reaction: 0.8s}
    variants:
      beginner:
        skill: {aim: 0.35, reaction: 1.4s}
        transitions:                                  # at Beginner they never flee
          - {from: engage, to: evade, when: "hit_recently(1s) and random(0.4)"}
          - {from: evade, to: engage, when: "time_in_state > 3s"}
      superhuman:
        skill: {aim: 0.9, reaction: 0.3s}
        states:
          engage: {range: 2km, fire_cone: 12, burst: 3s, lead: true}

docs.title: Difficulty variants (implemented)
docs.text:
Any definition — not only behaviours — can carry a variants: mapping with an entry per difficulty level, holding only the keys that differ; at that level the entry is merged over the definition (maps merge, lists and values replace). Levels are defined by the campaign ruleset (campaign: {difficulty: [beginner, experienced, veteran, genius, superhuman], default_difficulty: veteran} — the original's five), so a mod can have any number. (The earlier kind:id@level section idea was replaced by variants when the rules moved to YAML.)

A value that varies by difficulty does not need a variant: any number accepts one value per level, starting_money: {per_level: [5000000, 4500000, 4000000, 3500000, 3000000]}, as the original's Think.ini and *Goodies sections do (a shorter list repeats its last value).

docs.title: Built-in manoeuvres
docs.text: Implemented: idle, circle, patrol (circle round the spawn point), attack, evade, retreat (with jump), turret, tow. Design: the rest of this list. idle, patrol (route or area), formation (on a leader), attack (pursuit with firing discipline), strafe (attack runs on large targets), evade, retreat (to a point or hyperspace out), escort (stay near and defend), intercept (cut off a target before it reaches a point), tow (tug: tractor and haul a disabled ship), launch (carrier/freighter launching craft), turret (stationary aim and fire), mine (proximity trigger), probe (station-keeping with sensor/jamming effect), follow_path (convoy), dock. Each manoeuvre's parameters are documented with defaults. Wingmen use the same system with player orders as transitions ({from: "*", to: attack, when: "order(attack_my_target)"}; implemented so far as fixed wingman orders, with the class behaviour's attack parameters and skill).

docs.title: Weapon and equipment behaviours
docs.text: Weapons are behaviours too, with fewer states: a missile class names a guidance behaviour (homing, sidestep, dumbfire, cloaked_wait, decoy, cluster, proximity) with parameters; special equipment (ECM, cloak, tractor, VCT, damage control) names a built-in system with parameters. New combinations are data; new primitives need engine code or a Tier 2 hook.

docs.title: Tier 2: scripts
docs.text:
A Tier 1 definition can hand control to a script through a hook:

behaviours:
  portal_guardian:
    states:
      phase_3: {do: script, call: "scripts/guardian.lua:phase_3", every: 0.5s}

events:
  custom_ending:
    do: ["script(scripts/ending.lua:run)"]
  • Scripts see the same query and action API as Tier 1 (so nothing is reachable from a script that is not documented), run on the simulation tick, and must be deterministic (no clock, no files, no network; random numbers only from the game's generator).
  • Scripts may keep state only through the API (set_flag, counter, object variables), so saves never need to serialise a script VM.

docs.title: Language decision (Stage 3 entry)
docs.text:
Option Assessment Lua 5.4 via mlua (recommended) The modding standard; small, fast, sandboxable; MIT. Cost: a vendored C library and an FFI boundary, evaluated under the dependency policy. Rhai Pure Rust, MIT/Apache; slower; fewer modders know it. Grow Tier 1 into a full language No dependency, but loops, functions and tooling are the expensive part; rejected unless both candidates fail evaluation.

Because both shipped campaigns need only Tier 1, the choice can be made on its merits without blocking any campaign work.

docs.title: Format: campaign and game flow
docs.text: Status: design, except the difficulty levels (campaign: {difficulty, default_difficulty}), implemented in Stage 2; campaign: and starts: in Stage 4, arcs, plans, score and endings in Stage 5. The campaign ruleset is the top of a campaign mod: it says how a game starts, how time runs, which systems are switched on, how difficulty scales it, how it is scored and how it ends. Story progression is expressed with events and arcs (below); everything else is in the strategy rules.

docs.title: campaign:
docs.text:
# campaign/campaign.yaml (interceptor)
campaign:
  name: "X-COM: Interceptor"               # implemented (later a text key: "@campaign.name")
  difficulty: [beginner, experienced, veteran, genius, superhuman]   # implemented
  default_difficulty: veteran                                        # implemented
  # --- design (Stages 4 and 5) ---
  player: xcom                         # the player's faction
  start_date: 2067-01-01
  time_speeds: [5s, 1min, 5min, 30min, 1h, 24h]   # game time per real second, one per button
  pause: "event_priority >= high"      # auto-pause condition (see Reports)
  map: frontier                        # a generated or fixed star map
  start: interceptor                   # initial assets
  max_craft_per_mission: 5
  systems: [bases, research, manufacture, purchase, sell, pilots, probes, funding, salvage, capture]
  victory: "flag(doomsday_destroyed)"
  defeat:
    - {when: "flag(doomsday_complete)", ending: "@end.doomsday"}
    - {when: "count_bases(xcom) == 0", ending: "@end.last_base"}
    - {when: "flag(final_mission_failed)", ending: "@end.final_failed"}
  score: interceptor
  reports: [weekly, monthly]
  music: interceptor
  encyclopaedia: interceptor
Key Meaning player The faction the player commands. start_date, time_speeds, pause Calendar and the time-compression buttons; pause is a condition on events and messages. map A maps: definition: fixed or generated (strategy). start A starts: definition: bases, outposts, ships, pilots, stock, money, known research, relations. difficulty, default_difficulty Ordered level ids (any number) and the level a new game starts at. Implemented: every number in the mod may then be {per_level: [..]}, and any definition may have variants: {<level>: {…}} (behaviours). max_craft_per_mission Ships the player may launch on one mission. systems Strategy features in use. A campaign that omits research simply has no research screen; the default campaign uses them all, a pure dogfight campaign none. victory, defeat Conditions checked after every event and battle; the text key names the ending shown. victory may also be a list, each with its own ending (partial victories). score Score rules (below). reports Periodic reports. music, encyclopaedia Music sets and the in-game encyclopaedia (interface).

docs.title: Start state: starts: {<id>: …}
docs.text:
starts:
  interceptor:
    money: {per_level: [5000000, 4750000, 4500000, 3750000, 3000000]}
    bases: [{template: xcom_start, near: map_start}]
    outposts: {count: 3, near: base_1, faction: corporate}
    ships: {base_1: [lightning, lightning, lightning]}
    pilots: {base_1: {random: 5}}
    stock: {base_1: {sensor_probe: 5, xwinder: 10}}
    research_known: [laser_cannon, xwinder, conversion_drive]   # topics already complete
    rival: {bases: {count: 2, min_distance: 1pc}, outposts: 6, faction: alien}
    flags: []

A base template (base_templates: {xcom_start: …}) lists its modules by slot. near/distance place things on a generated map; a fixed map names systems instead.

docs.title: Arcs: story progression
docs.text:
The original's story is a gated chain: each step needs a date, earlier steps and campaign state, and opens the next activity. An arc expresses exactly that, and its steps are events:

arcs:
  doomsday:
    steps:
      - alien_message_1
      - alien_message_2
      - alien_message_3
      - alien_message_4
      - alien_message_5
      - summon_macarthur
      - final_mission

Each step fires once, only after the previous one, when its own when condition holds (dates, research, captures, chances per battle). The arc's state is visible to conditions (arc(doomsday) >= 3), so missions, the rival's plan and reports can depend on story progress. A campaign may have several arcs running in parallel (the default campaign has one main arc and side arcs for third parties).

docs.title: Rival plans: plans: {<id>: …}
docs.text:
The original's opponent pursues a project — the Doomsday device — built from components that must be shipped, which the player can intercept, and whose completion loses the game. The default campaign's villain has a plan of the same shape. A plan is a project with stages, costs, shipments and consequences:

plans:
  doomsday:
    owner: alien
    budget: think:financial/doomsday            # share of the owner's income (strategy rules)
    stages:
      - {component: structural, count: {per_level: [8, 9, 10, 7, 7]}, cost: 100000, ship: doomsday_freighter}
      - {component: weapon, count: {per_level: [8, 8, 8, 7, 6]}}
      - {component: drive, count: {per_level: [9, 8, 7, 6, 5]}}
    start_when: "arc(doomsday) >= 1"
    ship_visibility: {per_level: [65%, 60%, 55%, 50%, 45%]}   # chance a convoy passes within player sensors
    grant_if_missed: [structural, weapon]       # only at beginner, experienced, veteran (variants)
    complete: set_flag(doomsday_complete)
    warnings: {33%: dd_warning_1, 66%: dd_warning_2, 90%: dd_warning_3}

Conditions can read plan progress (plan(doomsday) as a fraction, plan_stage(doomsday)), so missions and events can trigger on how far the rival's development has gone — which is exactly what the default campaign's serial chapters need.

docs.title: Score: scores: {<id>: …}
docs.text:
scores:
  interceptor:
    events:
      alien_base_destroyed: 4500
      alien_outpost_destroyed: 2250
      outpost_defended: 2250
      base_lost: -5000
      refused_outpost_defence: -1500
      kill_fighter: [75, 200]          # by class rank
      salvage_item: item               # per item: the item's score key
    ratings: {phenomenal: 75000, excellent: 50000, very_good: 35000, good: 15000, ok: 0}
    feeds: funding                     # what the score drives (strategy rules)

Score events are named, so each original MissionScores index becomes a named entry (the index-to-meaning mapping is recovered in Stage 4 from the guide's table and play-testing).

docs.title: Reports: reports: {<id>: …}
docs.text: Periodic summaries (weekly news and advice, the monthly evaluation with funding changes) are reports: a period, the evaluation they run (strategy rules), and a text template with {variables} and conditional lines. News items are events with do: "news(@news.id)".

docs.title: Endings
docs.text: endings: {<id>: …}: text, image or video, music, and whether the game can continue (continue: false for defeats). Victory conditions name endings; the original has total and partial victory and three defeats.
